questions.question: Which of the following best describes a fibrillation potential recorded on needle EMG?
choices: Irregularly firing, polyphasic potential with a duration greater than 10 ms
A biphasic or triphasic potential with an initial negative deflection, firing irregularly
A regularly firing potential with an initial positive deflection, duration less than 5 ms, and amplitude up to about 1 mV
A waxing and waning potential in both amplitude and frequency
A grouped, repetitive burst discharge recurring at regular intervals
questions.explanation: Fibrillation potentials are the electrical signature of a single denervated muscle fiber discharging spontaneously. They are biphasic or triphasic with an initial POSITIVE deflection, fire with a regular, metronomic rhythm, have a duration under 5 ms, and an amplitude generally under about 1 mV. The initial positive deflection and regular firing pattern distinguish them from end-plate spikes (initial negative, irregular) and from fasciculations (irregular, motor-unit-sized).

questions.question: A needle positioned in the motor end-plate zone records brief, irregularly firing spikes that the patient describes as uncomfortable. What feature most reliably distinguishes these end-plate spikes from fibrillation potentials?
choices: End-plate spikes have a much longer duration than fibrillation potentials
End-plate spikes fire with a perfectly regular rhythm, while fibrillations are irregular
End-plate spikes have an initial negative deflection, while fibrillations have an initial positive deflection
End-plate spikes only occur in denervated muscle, while fibrillations occur in normal muscle
End-plate spikes have amplitudes exceeding 5 mV
questions.explanation: End-plate spikes represent irritation of intramuscular nerve terminals within the normal end-plate zone; they have an initial NEGATIVE deflection, fire irregularly, last 0.5 to 2 ms, and measure 10 to 50 microvolts. Fibrillation potentials, by contrast, have an initial POSITIVE deflection and fire regularly. This positive-versus-negative initial deflection is the single most reliable discriminator between the two, since both can otherwise appear similar in size and location within the muscle.

questions.question: Complex repetitive discharges (CRDs) are best characterized by which of the following?
choices: Gradual waxing and waning of amplitude and frequency
Abrupt onset and cessation with an unvarying, repeating waveform generated by ephaptic transmission
A single motor unit firing at 1 Hz to several times per minute
Continuous low-amplitude background noise resembling a seashell roar
Bursts of the same motor unit recurring every few seconds, as in myokymia
questions.explanation: CRDs arise when a group of denervated or diseased muscle fibers discharge synchronously through ephaptic (fiber-to-fiber) transmission rather than through normal neural activation. They start and stop abruptly (no gradual wax or wane, which instead characterizes myotonic discharges), and the waveform repeats itself identically from discharge to discharge, producing the classic machine-gun sound.

questions.question: Which finding on needle EMG is diagnostic of a myotonic discharge rather than a complex repetitive discharge?
choices: Abrupt onset and abrupt cessation of firing
An identical, unvarying waveform with each repetition
Progressive waxing and then waning of both amplitude and frequency, producing a dive-bomber sound
Firing rate that never exceeds 5 Hz
Occurrence exclusively in the motor end-plate zone
questions.explanation: Myotonic discharges characteristically wax and wane in BOTH amplitude and frequency, creating the classic dive-bomber or revving-motorcycle sound. This gradual change distinguishes them from CRDs, which have an abrupt on/off pattern with no wax or wane. Myotonic discharges are seen in myotonic dystrophy, myotonia congenita, and certain toxic or metabolic myopathies.

questions.question: A fasciculation potential differs from a fibrillation potential in which respect?
choices: Fasciculations have the configuration of a whole motor unit and fire irregularly, while fibrillations are single-fiber potentials that fire regularly
Fasciculations always indicate motor neuron disease, while fibrillations are always benign
Fasciculations have an initial positive deflection, while fibrillations have an initial negative deflection
Fasciculations can only be seen with concentric needles, while fibrillations require monopolar needles
Fasciculations have a duration under 5 ms, identical to fibrillations
questions.explanation: A fasciculation potential is the spontaneous, involuntary discharge of an entire motor unit (or part of one), so its morphology resembles a voluntary MUAP and it fires irregularly, anywhere from about 1 Hz to several times per minute. Fibrillation potentials, in contrast, arise from a single denervated muscle fiber, are much smaller and briefer, and fire with a regular rhythm. Fasciculations can be a normal (benign) finding or can indicate pathology such as ALS or radiculopathy; they are not diagnostic of disease in isolation.

questions.question: On the EMG monitor you see a large, complex, motor-unit-shaped discharge appearing at irregular, widely spaced intervals, alternating with much smaller, regularly firing biphasic spikes with an initial positive deflection. How should these two findings be classified?
choices: Both are fibrillation potentials at two different depths of needle insertion
The large, irregular discharge is a fasciculation potential; the small, regular, initial-positive discharge is a fibrillation potential
The large, irregular discharge is a positive sharp wave; the small, regular discharge is a myotonic discharge
Both represent end-plate activity at different distances from the end-plate zone
The large, irregular discharge is a CRD; the small, regular discharge is myokymia
questions.explanation: Size and firing pattern together identify these waveforms. A large discharge with normal motor-unit morphology firing irregularly and infrequently is a fasciculation potential (a spontaneously firing whole motor unit). A small, regularly firing, biphasic or triphasic potential with an initial positive deflection and duration under 5 ms is a fibrillation potential (a single denervated fiber). Recognizing both patterns simultaneously is common in active denervating disease such as radiculopathy or motor neuron disease.

questions.question: A motor nerve is stimulated at two points 260 mm apart. The onset latency at the distal site is 3.0 ms and at the proximal site is 7.0 ms. What is the calculated conduction velocity of the segment between the two stimulation sites?
questions.explanation: Conduction velocity equals distance divided by time, where time is the difference between the proximal and distal latencies (this isolates the segment between the two stimulation points, removing the fixed neuromuscular junction and terminal nerve delay common to both measurements). Here, the latency difference is 7.0 minus 3.0 = 4.0 ms, and the distance is 260 mm = 0.260 m. CV = 0.260 m divided by 0.004 s = 65 m/s.

questions.question: Why does the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) selectively reflect the function of only the largest, most rapidly conducting sensory axons in a nerve?
choices: Small fibers are unmyelinated and therefore produce no recordable potential at all
Slower-conducting fibers desynchronize in time as they travel, and their individually tiny contributions cancel out of the summated potential
Surface electrodes are physically unable to detect any fiber smaller than 10 micrometers in diameter
The stimulator delivers insufficient current to depolarize small fibers
Small fibers conduct sensory information only to the spinal cord, not peripherally
questions.explanation: The SNAP is a compound, summated potential produced by many individual sensory axons that reach the recording electrode over a range of conduction times. The fastest, large-diameter myelinated fibers arrive together and summate into the recordable peak. Slower fibers arrive at more varied, later times, so their small individual contributions become temporally dispersed and cancel out rather than adding to the recorded peak. As a result, the SNAP effectively reflects only the fastest, large myelinated sensory axons.

questions.question: When comparing a CMAP recorded from a suspected symptomatic limb to the same study performed on the asymptomatic contralateral limb, what side-to-side amplitude difference is generally considered abnormal?
choices: Side-to-side comparison is never clinically useful for CMAP
questions.explanation: Because normal individuals can show modest side-to-side variability in CMAP amplitude from technical factors alone, a difference greater than approximately 50 percent between limbs is generally required before it is considered a reliable indicator of an abnormality (typically axon loss) on the lower-amplitude side. Side-to-side comparison is a valuable tool, particularly in unilateral entrapment or traumatic lesions where a normal contralateral limb serves as the patient's own internal control.

questions.question: For routine antidromic sensory nerve conduction studies, what is generally considered the optimal distance between the active (G1) and reference (G2) recording electrodes?
choices: Distance between G1 and G2 has no effect on the recorded SNAP
questions.explanation: An inter-electrode distance of roughly 3 to 4 cm between the active and reference electrodes is generally recommended for sensory studies. This spacing is wide enough to avoid the reference electrode picking up a significant portion of the same signal as the active electrode (which would cancel out amplitude), while still being short enough to avoid excessive pickup of distant, unrelated electrical activity.

questions.question: If the reference electrode (G2) is moved too close to the active electrode (G1) during a sensory nerve conduction study, what is the expected effect on the recorded SNAP?
choices: Increased amplitude and increased peak latency
Decreased amplitude and a falsely shortened (earlier) peak latency
No change in amplitude, but a prolonged onset latency
Increased duration with no change in amplitude
Complete loss of the response with no measurable potential
questions.explanation: When G2 is placed too close to G1, it begins to detect a similar phase of the same traveling potential as G1, so the two electrodes partially cancel each other out (since the amplifier records the difference between them). This produces a falsely reduced amplitude and can make the peak appear to occur earlier than it truly would with proper electrode spacing, since the later phases of the waveform are being subtracted out.

questions.question: Increasing the low-frequency (high-pass) filter setting from 20 Hz to 100 Hz during a nerve conduction study will most likely have which effect on the recorded waveform?
choices: No change in amplitude or duration, only in onset latency
Increased amplitude with no change in duration
The waveform will be completely eliminated
questions.explanation: Raising the low-frequency filter removes more of the slow, low-frequency components of the signal. Since much of a nerve action potential's amplitude and later phases depend on these lower-frequency components, increasing the low-frequency filter blunts (decreases) the recorded amplitude and shortens the apparent duration of the waveform. This is a common technical pitfall in daily practice, since it can make a technically altered waveform mimic a pathologic finding such as axon loss.

questions.question: A patient's hand is unexpectedly cool during a median nerve conduction study. Compared to values obtained with proper limb warming, which pattern would this cooling most likely produce?
choices: Decreased amplitude, decreased duration, and increased conduction velocity
Increased amplitude, increased duration, and decreased conduction velocity
No change in amplitude or duration, but increased conduction velocity
Decreased amplitude with no effect on conduction velocity or duration
Increased conduction velocity with decreased distal latency
questions.explanation: Cooling slows the inactivation of sodium channels, which prolongs the time each fiber spends depolarized and increases temporal summation of individual fiber contributions to the compound potential. The net effect of a cold limb is an increase in amplitude, an increase in duration, and a decrease in conduction velocity (along with a prolonged distal latency). This counterintuitive pattern, larger but slower, is a classic clinical pitfall — always warm the limb before testing to avoid mistaking temperature effects for a demyelinating process.

questions.question: Approximately how much does upper limb motor conduction velocity decrease for each degree Celsius the limb temperature falls below 32 degrees C?
questions.explanation: A widely cited teaching figure is that upper limb conduction velocity falls by approximately 2.4 m/s for every degree Celsius the surface temperature drops below 32 degrees C. Distal latency, by comparison, prolongs by a smaller amount, approximately 0.2 ms per degree C of cooling. Because the effect on conduction velocity is substantial, limb warming (rather than applying a correction factor after the fact) is the preferred way to avoid a falsely abnormal study.

questions.question: What are the generally recommended minimum surface temperatures for performing nerve conduction studies in the upper and lower limbs, respectively?
choices: 28 degrees C upper limb, 26 degrees C lower limb
30 degrees C upper limb, 32 degrees C lower limb
32 degrees C upper limb, 30 degrees C lower limb
34 degrees C upper limb, 34 degrees C lower limb
Surface temperature does not need to be monitored if room temperature is comfortable
questions.explanation: The generally recommended minimum surface temperatures, measured with a skin thermometer, are approximately 32 degrees C for the upper limb (hand/forearm) and 30 degrees C for the lower limb (foot/leg), which is naturally somewhat cooler due to distance from the trunk. If the limb is found to be below these thresholds, the preferred correction is active warming of the limb prior to testing, not simply applying a mathematical correction factor to the raw data.

questions.question: A brief burst of electrical activity is recorded immediately after the needle is moved and then quickly subsides. Using a concentric needle electrode, what duration of this insertional activity is considered within normal limits?
choices: Insertional activity has no defined normal duration
questions.explanation: Normal insertional activity, the brief burst of spikes provoked by needle movement through muscle, should cease within about 300 ms of the needle coming to rest when using a concentric needle electrode (a slightly shorter threshold of about 230 ms is used for monopolar needles because of differences in the recording surface). Insertional activity that persists beyond this window suggests early or ongoing denervation, myotonia, or an inflammatory process.

questions.question: When measuring the duration of a motor unit action potential (MUAP) during needle EMG, which two points define the measurement?
choices: The onset of the first phase to the peak of the largest phase
The point where the waveform first departs from and last returns to the baseline
The interval between the two largest positive peaks
The time from the stimulus artifact to the first deflection
The width of the waveform measured at half of its maximal amplitude
questions.explanation: MUAP duration is measured from the point where the trace first clearly departs from the isoelectric baseline to the point where it definitively returns to baseline, including all of the low-amplitude components at the beginning and end of the potential. This measurement correlates with the number and spatial spread of muscle fibers belonging to that motor unit within the recording territory of the needle, making duration one of the most reproducible and clinically useful MUAP parameters.

questions.question: During a needle EMG examination, at approximately what firing rate does a normal motor unit typically reach before an additional motor unit is recruited to help generate more force?
questions.explanation: In a healthy muscle, an individual motor unit typically fires at about 5 to 10 Hz before the next motor unit is recruited to help generate additional force (the exact threshold varies somewhat with the muscle studied). This orderly relationship between firing rate and the number of units recruited is the basis of the recruitment ratio used to distinguish normal from neurogenic recruitment patterns.

questions.question: A patient with clinically apparent, profound weakness of ankle dorsiflexion is examined with needle EMG. Despite the patient's reported inability to generate force, the tibialis anterior shows a full, normal interference pattern with normal-appearing motor units whenever adequate effort is captured. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: A demyelinating conduction block proximal to the recording site
Non-organic (functional or psychogenic) weakness or poor voluntary effort, rather than a lower motor neuron lesion
A neuromuscular junction disorder such as myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Needle EMG assesses the motor unit pool directly and is not fooled by the patient's subjective effort in the way manual muscle testing can be. A full, normal recruitment/interference pattern with normal MUAP morphology in a muscle that appears clinically weak indicates that the lower motor neuron and muscle fiber apparatus are intact and capable of full activation; this pattern is characteristic of non-organic (functional or psychogenic) weakness, or of an upper motor neuron process, rather than any disorder of the peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction, or muscle itself.

questions.question: A patient presents with foot drop. Needle EMG shows abnormal spontaneous activity in the tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, posterior tibialis, and the L5 paraspinal muscles, with normal findings in the short head of biceps femoris. Which single muscle finding is most useful for localizing this lesion to the L5 root rather than the fibular nerve?
choices: Short head of biceps femoris abnormality
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus are innervated by the deep fibular nerve, so abnormalities there could reflect either an L5 radiculopathy or an isolated fibular neuropathy. Posterior tibialis, however, is innervated by the tibial nerve (L5 root) rather than the fibular nerve; finding it abnormal, together with paraspinal involvement, effectively excludes an isolated fibular neuropathy (which would spare a tibial-innervated muscle) and localizes the lesion to the L5 nerve root.

questions.question: A patient with neck pain radiating into the thumb and index finger is found to have a normal median sensory nerve action potential but a prolonged flexor carpi radialis H-reflex latency, along with denervation changes in the biceps, pronator teres, and cervical paraspinal muscles. What does the normal SNAP in this setting indicate?
choices: There is no nerve root pathology present
The lesion is distal to the dorsal root ganglion
The lesion is proximal to (or at) the dorsal root ganglion, that is, a preganglionic lesion typical of radiculopathy
The patient has a coexisting peripheral neuropathy masking the radiculopathy
The sensory fibers are more resistant to compression than motor fibers
questions.explanation: In a radiculopathy, the compressive lesion occurs proximal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), which lies within or near the intervertebral foramen. Because the sensory cell body (in the DRG) and its peripheral axon remain in continuity with the distal sensory nerve, the SNAP typically remains normal even when the patient has significant sensory symptoms. This is one of the most important localizing principles in electrodiagnosis: a preganglionic lesion (radiculopathy) spares the SNAP, while a postganglionic lesion (plexopathy or peripheral nerve lesion) does not.

questions.question: How does electrodiagnostic testing typically differentiate a brachial plexopathy from a cervical radiculopathy affecting a similar distribution of muscles?
choices: Paraspinal muscles are abnormal in both conditions
SNAPs are abnormal in brachial plexopathy (a postganglionic lesion) but normal in radiculopathy (a preganglionic lesion), assuming a comparable distribution
CMAPs are always normal in plexopathy but always abnormal in radiculopathy
F-waves are normal in plexopathy and abnormal in radiculopathy
There is no reliable electrodiagnostic way to distinguish the two conditions
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus lies distal to the dorsal root ganglion, so a plexopathy is a postganglionic lesion, unlike a radiculopathy, which is preganglionic. As a result, sensory nerve action potentials are reduced or absent in the affected distribution with a plexopathy, but remain normal with a radiculopathy. Paraspinal muscles, which are innervated by the dorsal rami very close to the spinal segment, are abnormal only in radiculopathy and are spared in plexopathy, providing a second complementary localizing clue.

questions.question: Needle EMG in a patient with chronic low back pain and a remote history of an L5 radiculopathy shows large-amplitude, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment in L5-innervated muscles, but no fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves. How should these findings be interpreted?
choices: Active, ongoing denervation of recent onset
A chronic, inactive (old) radiculopathy without current active denervation
Normal findings with no history of nerve injury
questions.explanation: Large-amplitude, long-duration, polyphasic MUAPs with reduced recruitment reflect chronic reinnervation, in which surviving motor axons have sprouted collateral branches to reinnervate muscle fibers left orphaned by earlier axon loss, a process that takes weeks to months to fully remodel. The absence of fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicates that there is no current, ongoing denervation, since these spontaneous potentials are the hallmark of active denervation. Together, this pattern, chronic neurogenic MUAP changes without active spontaneous activity, is the signature of an old, stable (inactive) radiculopathy.

questions.question: In the electrodiagnostic evaluation of a patient with foot drop, which combination of muscles is most useful for distinguishing an L5 radiculopathy from an isolated fibular (peroneal) neuropathy?
choices: Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis only
Posterior tibialis, tensor fasciae latae, and lumbar paraspinal muscles
Abductor hallucis and abductor digiti minimi pedis only
questions.explanation: Posterior tibialis (tibial nerve, L5) and tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve, L4-S1) are both L5-innervated muscles that are not supplied by the fibular nerve, so abnormalities in these muscles point away from an isolated fibular neuropathy and toward a more proximal L5 lesion. Lumbar paraspinal muscle involvement further localizes the lesion to the nerve root level (radiculopathy) rather than the plexus or peripheral nerve. Testing this combination, alongside the expected fibular-innervated muscles, is the standard strategy for working up foot drop.

questions.question: A patient develops foot drop and diminished ankle plantarflexion strength after a total hip arthroplasty, with EMG abnormalities in both fibular- and tibial-innervated muscles below the knee, though the fibular-innervated muscles are considerably more severely affected. What anatomic feature best explains why the fibular division is typically injured more severely than the tibial division in a sciatic nerve injury?
choices: The fibular division travels a shorter course and is therefore more exposed to stretch
The fibular division has less surrounding connective tissue and fewer fascicles, making it more vulnerable to compression and traction than the tibial division
The fibular division is purely sensory and therefore recovers more slowly
The tibial division lacks myelin, making it inherently more resistant to injury
The fibular division originates from lower lumbosacral roots than the tibial division and is therefore anatomically more distal
questions.explanation: Even though the fibular and tibial divisions travel together within a common sciatic nerve sheath through much of the thigh, the fibular (lateral trunk) division is more tightly bound with less surrounding connective tissue and fewer, larger fascicles than the tibial (medial trunk) division. This anatomic arrangement makes the fibular division disproportionately susceptible to compression, traction, and ischemic injury, which is why sciatic nerve injuries (from hip surgery, trauma, or prolonged compression) classically produce a clinical and electrodiagnostic picture that looks predominantly like a fibular neuropathy, even though the whole sciatic nerve is involved.

questions.question: In the electrodiagnostic evaluation of suspected mild carpal tunnel syndrome, the median wrist-to-palm short segment study is considered highly sensitive for detecting early focal slowing. What is the major technical limitation of this same short-segment technique?
choices: It cannot be performed with surface electrodes
It requires general anesthesia to perform accurately
Because the measured distance is short, small errors in distance measurement produce disproportionately large errors in the calculated conduction velocity
It can only be performed on the ulnar nerve, not the median nerve
It is insensitive to any degree of median neuropathy at the wrist
questions.explanation: The wrist-to-palm segment is typically only about 8 cm long, which makes it very sensitive to focal slowing across the carpal tunnel because there is little normal nerve included in the measurement to dilute a focal abnormality. However, this same short distance means that even small errors in caliper placement or measurement translate into proportionally large errors in the calculated latency-per-centimeter or conduction velocity, making meticulous technique essential when this segment is used.

questions.question: A patient with hand weakness and numbness of the palmar aspect of the small finger is found to have normal sensation over the dorsum of the hand on the ulnar side. This finding is most consistent with an ulnar nerve lesion at which location?
choices: The cubital tunnel at the elbow
questions.explanation: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises from the main ulnar nerve trunk proximal to the wrist, typically 5 to 8 cm proximal to the ulnar styloid, and it supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand on the ulnar side before the nerve enters Guyon's canal. A lesion at Guyon's canal (distal to this branch point) therefore spares dorsal hand sensation while still affecting the palmar cutaneous and deep motor branches. In contrast, a more proximal ulnar lesion (elbow, forearm, or plexus) would also involve the dorsal ulnar cutaneous territory.

questions.question: A positive Froment's sign, in which a patient flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint to compensate while pinching a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger, indicates weakness of which muscle and nerve?
choices: Flexor pollicis longus, weakened by a median nerve lesion
Abductor pollicis brevis, weakened by a median nerve lesion
Adductor pollicis, weakened by an ulnar nerve lesion
Opponens pollicis, weakened by a radial nerve lesion
First dorsal interosseous, weakened by a musculocutaneous nerve lesion
questions.explanation: Adductor pollicis, which provides the primary pinch (key pinch) force between the thumb and index finger, is innervated by the ulnar nerve (deep branch). When the ulnar nerve is injured, the patient recruits the median-innervated flexor pollicis longus to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint as a compensatory strategy to maintain grip on the paper, producing the visible thumb flexion known as Froment's sign, a clinical marker of ulnar nerve palsy.

questions.question: A long-distance cyclist develops numbness of the ring and small fingers along with hand intrinsic muscle weakness after a long ride, with sparing of sensation over the dorsum of the hand. This clinical scenario, sometimes called handlebar palsy, represents entrapment of which nerve at which location?
choices: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal from prolonged handlebar pressure
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
questions.explanation: Handlebar palsy refers to ulnar nerve compression at the wrist, within or near Guyon's canal, caused by prolonged pressure of the palm against a bicycle handlebar. Because the dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to Guyon's canal, dorsal hand sensation is spared, which helps distinguish this wrist-level lesion from a more proximal ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, where dorsal sensation would also be affected.

questions.question: True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome classically produces electrodiagnostic abnormalities most consistent with a lesion of which portion of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome results from chronic compression of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1), typically by a cervical rib or fibrous band. This produces a reduced or absent medial antebrachial cutaneous SNAP and ulnar SNAP, with a relatively preserved median SNAP, along with thenar-predominant hand intrinsic weakness and atrophy (sometimes called the Gilliatt-Sumner hand), reflecting the disproportionate involvement of the lower trunk's median nerve contribution to the thenar muscles.

questions.question: Which of the following nerves arises directly from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves as its terminal branches, along with the upper subscapular, lower subscapular, and thoracodorsal nerves more proximally. The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord, the ulnar and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves arise from the medial cord, and the dorsal scapular nerve arises directly from the C5 root, proximal to the trunks.

questions.question: The axillary nerve provides motor innervation to which muscles and carries sensation from which region?
choices: Biceps and brachialis; sensation from the lateral forearm
Deltoid and teres minor; sensation from a small patch over the lateral shoulder (the deltoid patch)
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus; no cutaneous sensory branch
Triceps and anconeus; sensation from the posterior forearm
Pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis; sensation from the palm
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve, arising from the posterior cord (C5-C6), innervates the deltoid and teres minor muscles and provides cutaneous sensation to a small patch of skin over the lateral aspect of the proximal shoulder (the deltoid patch, via the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm). It is commonly injured in anterior shoulder dislocations or proximal humerus fractures because of its close course around the surgical neck of the humerus.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the trunk-level origin of median nerve sensory versus motor fibers destined for the hand?
choices: Both sensory and motor median fibers arise exclusively from the lower trunk
Median sensory fibers to the hand travel primarily via the upper and middle trunks (lateral cord); median motor fibers to intrinsic hand muscles travel via the lower trunk (medial cord contribution)
Median sensory fibers arise from the posterior cord, while motor fibers arise from the lateral cord
Both sensory and motor median fibers arise exclusively from the upper trunk
The median nerve receives no contribution from the lower trunk under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The median nerve is formed by contributions from both the lateral cord (derived from the upper and middle trunks) and the medial cord (derived from the lower trunk). In general, the sensory fibers supplying the median-innervated digits travel predominantly through the upper and middle trunk to lateral cord pathway, while the motor fibers to the thenar and other intrinsic hand muscles travel predominantly through the lower trunk to medial cord pathway. This distinction is clinically useful when trying to localize a plexus lesion based on whether sensory or motor median-distribution deficits predominate.

questions.question: An infant sustains a traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus during a difficult delivery. Which muscle group would be expected to be weak, producing the classic waiter's tip posture?
choices: Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps, producing shoulder adduction/internal rotation and elbow extension posturing
Flexor digitorum profundus and flexor carpi ulnaris
Only the muscles innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve
questions.explanation: Upper trunk (C5-C6) injury, classically from shoulder dystocia or a fall onto the shoulder, is known as Erb's palsy. It weakens the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps, resulting in an arm that hangs adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, the classic waiter's tip posture. This contrasts with Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8-T1), which affects the hand intrinsic muscles and may be accompanied by a Horner's syndrome.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve is formed from which nerve roots and consists of which two divisions traveling together within a common sheath?
choices: S1-S4; pudendal and inferior gluteal divisions
L4-S1; superior and inferior gluteal divisions
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve arises from the L4 through S3 nerve roots and is actually composed of two distinct divisions, the tibial (medial) division and the fibular/peroneal (lateral) division, bundled together within a common connective tissue sheath from the pelvis through most of the thigh before typically separating near the popliteal fossa. Understanding this dual composition is essential for interpreting sciatic nerve injuries, since the two divisions can be affected unequally.

questions.question: The obturator nerve arises from which nerve roots, from which rami, and exits the pelvis through which structure?
choices: L2-L4, posterior rami, through the greater sciatic foramen
L2-L4, anterior rami, through the obturator foramen
L4-S1, posterior rami, through the piriformis muscle
T12-L1, anterior rami, through the inguinal canal
L1-L3, posterior rami, through the femoral triangle
questions.explanation: The obturator nerve arises from the anterior rami of L2 through L4 (in contrast to the femoral nerve, which arises from the posterior divisions of the same root levels), and it exits the pelvis through the obturator foramen to reach the medial thigh, where it innervates the hip adductor muscles (adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, and part of adductor magnus).

questions.question: A patient develops acute anterior thigh weakness and numbness after undergoing femoral artery catheterization. Which anatomic relationship explains the femoral nerve's vulnerability to injury during this procedure?
choices: The femoral nerve pierces directly through the femoral artery
The femoral nerve runs immediately lateral to the femoral artery within the femoral triangle, making it susceptible to compression from a hematoma or direct needle trauma
The femoral nerve has no fixed anatomic relationship to the femoral vessels
The femoral nerve runs posterior to the femoral vein, far from the arterial puncture site
The femoral nerve is protected from injury by the inguinal ligament in all cases
questions.explanation: Within the femoral triangle, the femoral nerve lies just lateral to the femoral artery (which in turn lies lateral to the femoral vein, following the mnemonic NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics, from lateral to medial). This close proximity makes the femoral nerve vulnerable to compression by a retroperitoneal or groin hematoma, or to direct needle injury, during femoral artery catheterization procedures such as cardiac catheterization.

questions.question: During median motor nerve conduction studies recording from the hypothenar (ulnar-innervated) muscles, stimulation of the median nerve at the elbow produces an unexpected volume-conducted response with an initial positive deflection. What anomalous connection does this finding suggest?
choices: A Martin-Gruber anastomosis, a median-to-ulnar motor fiber crossover in the forearm
A Riche-Cannieu anastomosis in the hand only
Bilateral absence of the ulnar nerve
A congenital absence of the median nerve
questions.explanation: A Martin-Gruber anastomosis is an anomalous communication in which motor axons cross from the median nerve (or its anterior interosseous branch) to the ulnar nerve within the forearm, present in roughly 15 to 30 percent of the general population. When present, stimulating the median nerve proximally while recording over ulnar-innervated hypothenar muscle can pick up a volume-conducted response, sometimes with an initial positive deflection, from muscle fibers that are actually reached via the anomalous median-to-ulnar pathway. Recognizing this anomaly is important because it can also produce a pseudo-conduction-block appearance on standard ulnar conduction studies that must not be mistaken for pathology.

questions.question: An accessory deep peroneal nerve, present in up to what percentage of the population, provides additional motor innervation to which muscle, and follows what course?
choices: Up to 5 percent; innervates tibialis anterior; courses anterior to the medial malleolus
Up to 28 percent; innervates the lateral portion of extensor digitorum brevis; courses posterior to the lateral malleolus
Up to 50 percent; innervates abductor hallucis; courses through the tarsal tunnel
Up to 15 percent; innervates gastrocnemius; courses through the popliteal fossa
Up to 28 percent; innervates the medial portion of extensor digitorum brevis; courses anterior to the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: An accessory deep peroneal (fibular) nerve is present in up to about 28 percent of the population. It arises as a branch of the superficial fibular nerve and travels posterior to (behind) the lateral malleolus before turning to supply the lateral portion of the extensor digitorum brevis muscle, a portion of that muscle not reached by the standard deep fibular nerve pathway at the ankle.

questions.question: A peroneal motor study recording from extensor digitorum brevis shows a larger CMAP amplitude with stimulation at the fibular head than with stimulation at the ankle, raising concern for a conduction block. What additional maneuver would help confirm an accessory deep peroneal nerve as the explanation rather than true pathology?
choices: Repeating the ankle stimulation at a lower stimulus intensity
Stimulating just posterior to the lateral malleolus while continuing to record from extensor digitorum brevis, looking for a response that accounts for the amplitude difference
Switching the recording electrode to the tibialis anterior muscle
Performing sensory conduction studies of the superficial fibular nerve only
Repeating the study with the limb cooled to 25 degrees C
questions.explanation: Because the accessory deep peroneal nerve travels posterior to the lateral malleolus before reaching extensor digitorum brevis, stimulating directly over that course, just behind and below the lateral malleolus, while still recording from extensor digitorum brevis will elicit an additional response. If the amplitude obtained at this accessory site, when added to the standard ankle response, accounts for the amplitude recorded with more proximal (fibular head) stimulation, this confirms an anomalous accessory deep peroneal nerve rather than a true conduction block or axon loss lesion.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes axonotmesis in the Seddon classification of nerve injury?
choices: The axon remains intact while only the myelin sheath is disrupted, with no Wallerian degeneration
The axon is disrupted and undergoes Wallerian degeneration, but the surrounding connective tissue framework is preserved, allowing organized regeneration
All neural and connective tissue elements are completely disrupted, precluding any spontaneous recovery
Only sensory axons are affected, while motor axons remain fully functional
Recovery occurs within hours because no axonal disruption has occurred
questions.explanation: Axonotmesis describes an injury in which the axon itself is disrupted and undergoes Wallerian degeneration distal to the lesion, but the surrounding connective tissue scaffolding, particularly the endoneurial tubes, remains largely intact. This preserved framework allows regenerating axon sprouts to find their way back to the correct distal target, so recovery, although it takes time (regeneration proceeds at roughly 1 mm per day), is generally good.

questions.question: A patient develops acute wrist drop after falling asleep with their arm draped over a chair (Saturday night palsy). Nerve conduction studies performed one week later show a conduction block across the spiral groove with normal amplitudes and normal needle EMG both proximal and distal to the lesion, without fibrillation potentials. This pattern is most consistent with which type of nerve injury?
choices: Neurapraxia, a focal conduction block without axonal disruption
questions.explanation: Neurapraxia represents a focal conduction block caused by localized myelin injury (often from compression) without disruption of the underlying axon. Because the axon remains intact, there is no Wallerian degeneration, so distal stimulation continues to produce a normal-amplitude response, and needle EMG does not show fibrillation potentials. Neurapraxia carries the best prognosis of all nerve injury types, typically resolving within days to a few weeks as the local myelin injury heals.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes neurotmesis from axonotmesis?
choices: Neurotmesis involves disruption of the axon and all surrounding connective tissue layers, including the epineurium, so spontaneous meaningful recovery does not occur without surgical repair
Neurotmesis has a better prognosis than axonotmesis because regeneration occurs more quickly
Neurotmesis spares the axon entirely, affecting only the myelin sheath
Neurotmesis is diagnosed exclusively by needle EMG, never by nerve conduction studies
Neurotmesis and axonotmesis are managed identically in all cases
questions.explanation: Neurotmesis is the most severe grade of nerve injury, corresponding to Sunderland's fifth degree, in which the axon and all supporting connective tissue layers (endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium) are completely disrupted, as occurs with a full nerve transection. Because the connective tissue scaffolding that would normally guide regenerating axons back to their targets is destroyed, spontaneous, functionally meaningful recovery does not occur, and surgical repair (direct repair or grafting) is generally required to achieve any recovery.

questions.question: Following a complete axonotmetic injury to the median nerve at the elbow, which finding would be expected on needle EMG of the abductor pollicis brevis within the first 24 to 48 hours, before fibrillation potentials have had time to develop?
choices: Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves throughout the muscle
Reduced recruitment of motor unit potentials, with normal MUAP morphology, and no spontaneous activity yet
Complete electrical silence with no MUAPs and no spontaneous activity
Increased insertional activity with trains of positive sharp waves
questions.explanation: Immediately after an axonotmetic injury, before Wallerian degeneration has progressed far enough to produce spontaneous fibrillation potentials (which take about 10 to 14 days to appear in proximal muscles and 3 to 4 weeks in more distal muscles such as the intrinsic hand muscles), the earliest detectable needle EMG abnormality is reduced recruitment: because a portion of the motor axon pool can no longer drive the muscle, fewer motor units are available to be recruited voluntarily, even though the MUAPs that are present still look morphologically normal at this early stage.

questions.question: Repetitive nerve stimulation at 2 to 3 Hz in a patient with suspected myasthenia gravis characteristically shows what pattern, and what does it reflect about the underlying pathophysiology?
choices: A progressive increment of over 100 percent, reflecting a presynaptic defect in acetylcholine release
A decrement greater than 10 percent between the first and a subsequent response, reflecting a postsynaptic reduction in available acetylcholine receptors
No change at all, since myasthenia gravis does not affect repetitive stimulation
A decrement that only appears at high stimulation frequencies above 20 Hz
An increment that normalizes the resting CMAP amplitude
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder caused by antibodies directed against the acetylcholine receptor (or, in a subset of patients, against muscle-specific kinase). With slow, low-frequency repetitive stimulation at 2 to 3 Hz, progressive depletion of the readily releasable acetylcholine pool combined with a reduced number of postsynaptic receptors causes a progressively smaller endplate potential with each stimulus, producing a decrement greater than 10 percent (typically comparing the fourth or fifth response to the first). Resting CMAP amplitude is usually normal in myasthenia gravis, and thymoma is a well-recognized association.

questions.question: A patient presents with proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, and diminished deep tendon reflexes that improve after brief voluntary exercise. Nerve conduction studies show low resting CMAP amplitudes that increase by more than 100 percent following 10 seconds of maximal voluntary contraction. What is the most likely diagnosis and its most important associated malignancy?
choices: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome; associated with small cell lung cancer
Guillain-Barre syndrome; not associated with malignancy
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder caused by antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels, which impair calcium-dependent acetylcholine vesicle release. The hallmark electrodiagnostic findings are a low resting CMAP amplitude and a marked incremental response, typically greater than 100 percent, following brief exercise or rapid (20 to 50 Hz) repetitive stimulation, as accumulating intracellular calcium transiently overcomes the presynaptic defect. LEMS is strongly associated with small cell lung cancer as a paraneoplastic phenomenon, making malignancy screening an essential part of the workup.

questions.question: A previously healthy 3-month-old infant develops constipation, followed over several days by poor feeding, a weak cry, hypotonia, and diminished deep tendon reflexes. Which diagnosis should be strongly suspected?
questions.explanation: Infantile botulism results from ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores (classically associated with honey), which then colonize the infant's immature gastrointestinal tract and produce botulinum toxin locally. Constipation is often the earliest sign, typically preceding the descending, symmetric weakness that follows, including poor feeding, weak cry, bulbar weakness, hypotonia, and diminished reflexes, reflecting the toxin's presynaptic blockade of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Electrodiagnostically, botulism produces a pattern similar to LEMS, with low CMAP amplitudes and an incremental response to rapid repetitive stimulation.

questions.question: In neuromuscular junction physiology, the term safety factor refers to which of the following concepts?
choices: The maximum firing rate a motor neuron can sustain without fatigue
The ratio of acetylcholine released per nerve impulse to the minimum amount needed to reach the threshold for generating a muscle fiber action potential
The number of synaptic vesicles present in the presynaptic terminal at rest
The distance between the nerve terminal and the postsynaptic membrane
The percentage of muscle fibers within a motor unit that are type I versus type II
questions.explanation: The safety factor of neuromuscular transmission describes the normal physiologic excess of acetylcholine released with each nerve impulse relative to the minimum quantity required to depolarize the postsynaptic membrane to threshold and reliably trigger a muscle fiber action potential. This built-in margin ensures reliable transmission under normal circumstances. Disorders of the neuromuscular junction, whether they reduce postsynaptic receptor number (myasthenia gravis), impair presynaptic release (Lambert-Eaton syndrome), or block release entirely (botulism), all ultimately act by eroding this safety factor, which is why transmission failure and clinical fatigability are common final pathways across these otherwise distinct diseases.

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, and botulism differ in whether the defect is presynaptic or postsynaptic, yet they share what common underlying mechanism that produces their clinical and electrodiagnostic features?
choices: All three cause irreversible destruction of the muscle fiber membrane
All three result in a reduced safety factor of neuromuscular transmission, leading to intermittent or progressive failure of individual endplate potentials to reach threshold
All three are caused by the same autoantibody
All three exclusively affect ocular muscles
All three produce permanent axonal loss on nerve conduction studies
questions.explanation: Despite affecting different steps in the process (postsynaptic receptor availability in myasthenia gravis, presynaptic calcium-mediated vesicle release in Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and presynaptic vesicle docking and release via SNARE protein cleavage in botulism), all neuromuscular junction disorders converge on the same final common pathway: a reduced safety factor. When the margin between the acetylcholine released and the threshold needed for a muscle fiber action potential narrows enough, individual endplate potentials intermittently or progressively fail to trigger a muscle fiber response, producing the clinical fatigability and the characteristic decremental or incremental repetitive stimulation patterns used to diagnose these conditions.

questions.question: Which set of characteristics correctly describes the F-wave?
choices: Elicited by submaximal stimulation, constant latency, amplitude equal to the CMAP
Elicited by supramaximal stimulation, variable latency and morphology from trial to trial, amplitude approximately 1 to 5 percent of the CMAP
A true monosynaptic spinal reflex requiring an intact afferent sensory pathway
Present only in demyelinating polyneuropathy and absent in normal individuals
Generated by orthodromic conduction along sensory fibers only
questions.explanation: The F-wave is produced by antidromic activation of a variable subpopulation of anterior horn motor neurons following a supramaximal stimulus; because a different, somewhat random group of motor neurons backfires with each stimulus, both the latency and the morphology of the F-wave vary noticeably from trial to trial. Its amplitude is small, typically only about 1 to 5 percent of the corresponding CMAP amplitude. Because the same motor axon carries the impulse both antidromically and then orthodromically back out, it is not a true reflex and does not require any sensory (afferent) pathway.

questions.question: Compared to the F-wave, the H-reflex is characterized by which of the following?
choices: Supramaximal stimulation and highly variable latency
Submaximal stimulation, with stable, reproducible latency and amplitude from trial to trial, reflecting a true monosynaptic reflex arc
Complete absence of any afferent (sensory) component
An amplitude that is typically larger than the CMAP
A firing pattern that waxes and wanes with each successive stimulus
questions.explanation: The H-reflex is the electrophysiologic correlate of a tendon stretch reflex, mediated by a true monosynaptic reflex arc: a submaximal stimulus preferentially activates large-diameter group Ia sensory afferents, which synapse directly on alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord, producing a motor response. Because it follows a fixed anatomic reflex pathway rather than the somewhat random antidromic backfiring that generates the F-wave, the H-reflex has a stable, reproducible latency and amplitude from stimulus to stimulus. The most commonly tested H-reflex sites are the tibial nerve and soleus muscle (assessing the S1 root) and the median nerve and flexor carpi radialis (assessing C6-C7).

questions.question: An extra late response is noted on a nerve conduction study, occurring at a constant latency and with constant morphology on every trial, typically situated between the M-wave and the F-wave. At what stimulus intensity is this response, known as an A-wave or axon reflex, typically best elicited?
choices: Supramaximal stimulation only, identical to that used for F-waves
It cannot be elicited with surface stimulation
Only with stimulation of purely sensory nerves
questions.explanation: The A-wave, or axon reflex, arises from an anomalous or collateral branch point along the motor axon's course where the impulse can reflect or take an alternate route back toward the muscle. Unlike the F-wave, the A-wave has a constant latency and morphology with repeated stimulation, since it results from a fixed anatomic pathway rather than variable motor neuron backfiring. It is most consistently and clearly elicited at moderate, submaximal stimulus intensities; at supramaximal intensities it may become obscured by or merge with the F-wave. Its presence can be a subtle marker of peripheral nerve pathology, such as an early polyneuropathy or a reinnervating lesion.

questions.question: In the blink reflex, the R1 and R2 components differ in which important way?
choices: R1 is bilateral and polysynaptic; R2 is ipsilateral and oligosynaptic

R1 is an early, ipsilateral, oligosynaptic response (trigeminal afferent to the pons to the facial nerve); R2 is a later, bilateral, polysynaptic response (trigeminal afferent to the medulla with bilateral connections to both facial nerve nuclei)
Both R1 and R2 are always bilateral and appear at identical latencies
R1 assesses only the facial nerve, with no trigeminal (afferent) component
R2 is faster than R1 in every normal individual
questions.explanation: The blink reflex is elicited by stimulating the supraorbital branch of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) and recording from the orbicularis oculi muscles bilaterally. The R1 response is an early, ipsilateral, oligosynaptic response mediated through a pathway from the trigeminal afferent to the main sensory trigeminal nucleus in the pons and then to the ipsilateral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) nucleus. The R2 response is later and polysynaptic, relaying through the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the medulla, which projects bilaterally to both facial nerve nuclei, producing a response on both the stimulated and unstimulated sides. This bilateral R2 makes the blink reflex useful for localizing lesions anywhere along the trigeminal afferent pathway, the brainstem interneuron pathway, or either facial nerve efferent pathway.

questions.question: A neurogenic process causing loss of functioning motor units produces which characteristic pattern on needle EMG during a voluntary contraction?
choices: Early recruitment of small, short-duration motor units
Reduced recruitment (fewer motor units activated) with an increased firing rate of the remaining units, as they compensate for the reduced number of available units
A completely silent interference pattern regardless of effort
Normal recruitment with normal MUAP morphology
Decreased firing rate of the remaining motor units despite maximal effort
questions.explanation: When axon loss reduces the total number of functioning motor units available to a muscle, the remaining motor units must each fire at a faster rate to generate the force that would normally be produced by a full complement of units. This produces the classic neurogenic pattern: reduced recruitment (fewer distinct motor units seen or heard on the interference pattern) combined with an increased firing rate of those units that remain, sometimes described as a rapid, picket-fence firing pattern when very few units remain.

questions.question: Which motor unit and recruitment pattern is characteristic of a myopathic process?
choices: Large-amplitude, long-duration motor units with reduced recruitment
Small-amplitude, short-duration, polyphasic motor units recruited early, that is, with more units activated than expected for the force being generated
Absence of any motor unit potentials even with maximal effort
Normal-amplitude motor units firing at an abnormally slow rate
Giant motor units with markedly increased duration and reduced recruitment
questions.explanation: In myopathic disorders, individual muscle fibers are lost or dysfunctional within otherwise intact motor units, so each motor unit generates less force than normal. To produce a given level of force, the nervous system must recruit a greater number of these weakened motor units earlier (at a lower effort threshold) than would normally be needed, a pattern called early or rapid recruitment. The individual MUAPs themselves are typically small in amplitude, short in duration, and often polyphasic, reflecting the reduced number of functioning muscle fibers within each motor unit's territory.

questions.question: With respect to motor unit action potential parameters, which statement correctly distinguishes what duration and amplitude each primarily reflect?
choices: Duration reflects fiber density immediately adjacent to the needle tip, while amplitude reflects the total number of fibers in the motor unit

Duration reflects the total number of muscle fibers belonging to the motor unit within the needle's recording territory, while amplitude primarily reflects the fibers located immediately adjacent to the recording electrode
Duration and amplitude both measure exactly the same underlying physiologic property and are therefore redundant
Duration is determined solely by the conduction velocity of the fastest fiber in the motor unit
Amplitude reflects the number of phases in the motor unit potential
questions.explanation: MUAP duration reflects the temporal and spatial spread of all the muscle fibers belonging to a given motor unit that lie within the pick-up territory of the recording needle, making it a good overall reflection of the number of fibers in that unit. MUAP amplitude, by contrast, is dominated by the one or few muscle fibers located immediately adjacent to the needle's recording surface (fiber density in that immediate vicinity), since amplitude falls off very steeply with distance from the electrode. This is why duration is generally considered a more representative, reproducible parameter of overall motor unit size than amplitude.

questions.question: A patient with a remote history of paralytic poliomyelitis decades earlier undergoes needle EMG. Which pattern would be the classic expected finding?
choices: Small, short-duration, polyphasic motor units with early recruitment, identical to a myopathy
Large-amplitude, long-duration motor units with reduced recruitment, and few or no fibrillation potentials, reflecting fully remodeled chronic reinnervation
Abundant fibrillation potentials with normal-sized motor units and normal recruitment
A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
Myotonic discharges throughout the affected muscles
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis causes acute destruction of anterior horn cells, followed, in surviving motor neurons, by extensive collateral sprouting to reinnervate muscle fibers left orphaned by the destroyed neurons. Decades later, this process has fully remodeled the motor units into very large, long-duration, often giant potentials, reflecting the greatly expanded territory of the surviving units. Because the process is old and stable rather than actively ongoing, fibrillation potentials are typically few or absent, while recruitment remains reduced because of the permanently diminished number of functioning motor units. This chronic, stable, purely neurogenic pattern is a classic teaching example distinct from an active, ongoing denervating process.

questions.question: In a patient presenting within the first several days of an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP, Guillain-Barre syndrome), routine motor and sensory nerve conduction studies of the limbs may still appear largely normal. What is typically the earliest electrodiagnostic abnormality to appear?
choices: Marked slowing of forearm conduction velocity
Absent or prolonged F-waves, and/or absent H-reflexes, reflecting early proximal (root and plexus level) demyelination
Reduced SNAP amplitudes in all four limbs
Fibrillation potentials throughout all limb muscles
A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
questions.explanation: In AIDP, the earliest sites of inflammatory demyelination are often the spinal nerve roots and proximal plexus, regions not well assessed by standard distal motor and sensory conduction studies. Because F-waves and the H-reflex both traverse these proximal segments, absent or prolonged F-waves and absent H-reflexes are typically the earliest detectable electrodiagnostic abnormalities, sometimes preceding any changes in distal latency, conduction velocity, or amplitude by several days. Conduction block, temporal dispersion, and more widespread slowing typically emerge later, over the first one to two weeks of the illness.

questions.question: A slowly progressive, distal, sensory-predominant neuropathy in an older man is found to have an IgM monoclonal gammopathy and antibodies against myelin-associated glycoprotein (anti-MAG). Which electrodiagnostic feature is classically disproportionately affected in this condition?
choices: Conduction velocity, which is only mildly reduced
F-wave latency, which is entirely normal
Distal motor latencies, which are severely and disproportionately prolonged relative to the degree of conduction velocity slowing
SNAP amplitude, which remains entirely normal in all cases
Insertional activity, which is markedly reduced
questions.explanation: Anti-MAG neuropathy (sometimes classified as distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy, or DADS) is characteristically associated with severe, disproportionate prolongation of distal motor latencies, often out of proportion to the relatively milder slowing seen in forearm or leg conduction velocities. This distal-predominant pattern, together with the associated IgM paraproteinemia, is a classic and frequently tested combination that helps distinguish anti-MAG neuropathy from other acquired and hereditary demyelinating polyneuropathies.

questions.question: When comparing a hereditary demyelinating neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 to an acquired demyelinating neuropathy such as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), which electrodiagnostic feature most reliably favors the hereditary diagnosis?
choices: Presence of fibrillation potentials, which occur only in hereditary neuropathy
Uniform slowing of conduction velocity across multiple nerves and segments, without conduction block or significant temporal dispersion
Markedly asymmetric involvement between the two sides of the body
Isolated involvement of a single nerve with sparing of all others
A decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
questions.explanation: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathies such as CMT1 result from a generalized, genetically determined abnormality of myelin present in essentially all peripheral nerve fibers from an early age, so conduction slowing tends to be uniform across different nerves and along different segments of the same nerve, typically without conduction block or significant temporal dispersion. Acquired demyelinating neuropathies such as CIDP, by contrast, result from a patchy, multifocal immune-mediated attack on myelin, producing non-uniform slowing that varies from segment to segment and nerve to nerve, often with conduction block and temporal dispersion at the sites of active demyelination. This uniform-versus-patchy distinction is one of the most important tools for differentiating hereditary from acquired demyelinating polyneuropathies electrodiagnostically.

questions.question: MUAP duration primarily reflects:
choices: Number of muscle fibers nearest the electrode
Total number of muscle fibers in the motor unit
questions.explanation: Duration reflects the total number of muscle fibers contributing to the motor unit, measured from baseline departure to return. Amplitude (not duration) reflects the fibers nearest the electrode.

questions.question: Which MUAP parameter reflects only the 2-12 muscle fibers closest to the recording electrode?
questions.explanation: Amplitude is a high-frequency component, and tissue acts as a high-frequency filter, so only the closest 2 to 12 fibers contribute meaningfully to the recorded amplitude.

questions.question: A rise time greater than 500 microseconds on needle EMG indicates:
choices: The motor unit is abnormally large
The needle is too far from the motor unit being studied
questions.explanation: A rise time greater than 500µs means the needle is not close enough to the motor unit. Reposition the needle before analyzing MUAP parameters such as amplitude and duration.

questions.question: In early reinnervation, nascent motor units differ from myopathic MUAPs because nascent units have:
questions.explanation: Both nascent and myopathic MUAPs are short, small, and polyphasic, but nascent units have REDUCED recruitment (fewer available motor units) while myopathic units have early or normal recruitment.

questions.question: What percentage of MUAPs in the deltoid muscle can normally be polyphasic?
questions.explanation: The deltoid is a notable exception where up to 25% polyphasic MUAPs is considered normal, compared with greater than 10% being abnormal in most other muscles.

questions.question: What is the normal MUAP recruitment ratio?
questions.explanation: Recruitment ratio equals the firing rate of the first MUAP divided by the number of MUAPs firing. Normal is approximately 5:1.

questions.question: Satellite potentials during needle EMG are most characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Satellite potentials are small, time-locked potentials trailing the main MUAP, caused by slow conduction in immature collateral sprouts during early reinnervation.

questions.question: In the recommended technique for ulnar motor NCS, what elbow position should be used?
questions.explanation: A flexed elbow position (70-90 degrees) is more sensitive for detecting ulnar neuropathy at the elbow than an extended position.

questions.question: A patient with weakness of all ulnar-innervated hand muscles but intact sensation over the dorsum of the hand most likely has a lesion at:
questions.explanation: Guyon's canal Type 3 affects the deep palmar and hypothenar motor branches. The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist and is spared.

questions.question: The most common site of radial nerve injury is:
questions.explanation: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove ('Saturday Night Palsy') is the most common radial nerve injury, typically from prolonged compression during deep sleep or intoxication.

questions.question: A patient with wrist drop and radial deviation has which of these localized lesions?
choices: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
questions.explanation: A PIN lesion spares the ECRL (innervated proximal to the Arcade of Frohse), so wrist extension is weak but deviates radially. In spiral groove or axilla lesions, the wrist drops without radial deviation.

questions.question: When recording the tibial motor NCS from the abductor hallucis, the active electrode is placed:
choices: Two finger widths distal to the navicular bone on the medial foot
On the dorsum of the foot
questions.explanation: The abductor hallucis recording site uses the belly-tendon method, with G1 on the medial foot, two finger widths distal to the navicular bone.

questions.question: The sural nerve receives contributions primarily from which nerve?
choices: Primarily tibial with some deep peroneal
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is formed primarily from the tibial nerve via the sural communicating branch, with some contribution from the deep peroneal nerve.

questions.question: The only muscle above the knee innervated by the peroneal division of the sciatic nerve is the:
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris is innervated by the peroneal portion of the sciatic nerve; the long head is innervated by the tibial portion. This makes it crucial for localizing peroneal vs sciatic lesions.

questions.question: A patient presents with foot drop. EMG of the short head of biceps femoris is normal. The lesion is most likely at:
choices: Common peroneal nerve at fibular head
questions.explanation: A normal short head of biceps femoris (innervated by the peroneal division above the knee) localizes the lesion to the fibular head or below.

questions.question: In carpal tunnel syndrome, which study is usually the FIRST to become abnormal?
questions.explanation: Sensory studies are the first to become abnormal and the most sensitive for detecting carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: When comparing median and ulnar sensory studies from the ring finger for CTS diagnosis, what latency difference is considered abnormal?
questions.explanation: A difference greater than 0.5ms in distal latency between median and ulnar antidromic sensory studies from the 4th digit is abnormal and supports carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: Anterior interosseous syndrome is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Weakness of FPL and FDP to digits 2-3
questions.explanation: AIN is a pure motor nerve, so sensory NCS (SNAPs) are normal. Patients cannot flex the DIP of the index/middle fingers or the IP of the thumb.

questions.question: Normal distal latency for the facial motor nerve study is:
questions.explanation: Normal facial motor distal latency is 3-4 ms with amplitude 1-4 mV, recorded from orbicularis oculi.

questions.question: In the blink reflex, the R1 component has a normal latency of:
questions.explanation: R1 is 8-13 ms and appears only ipsilaterally. R2 is 28-42 ms ipsilaterally and R2c is 29-44 ms contralaterally.

questions.question: The blink reflex tests which two cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The blink reflex has an afferent arc via the trigeminal nerve (CN V, supraorbital branch) and an efferent arc via the facial nerve (CN VII).

questions.question: In NCS, conduction block is defined as a drop in CMAP area or amplitude of at least:
questions.explanation: Conduction block requires at least a 50% drop in CMAP area or amplitude between distal and proximal stimulation sites.

questions.question: A patient with a demyelinating polyneuropathy has preserved sural sensory responses but abnormal median and ulnar sensory responses. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The 'sural sparing pattern' (preserved sural SNAP with abnormal upper extremity SNAPs) is characteristic of CIDP.

questions.question: NCS only test which type of nerve fibers?
choices: Both large and small fibers equally
questions.explanation: Standard NCS only assess large, fast-conducting myelinated fibers. Small fiber neuropathies can have entirely normal electrodiagnostic studies.

questions.question: Which of these correctly describes F-wave characteristics?
choices: Supramaximal stimulus, variable latency and morphology
questions.explanation: F-waves use supramaximal stimulation and have variable latency and morphology trial-to-trial because different motor neurons backfire each time. About 1-5% of motor neurons fire on each trial.

questions.question: In a patient with 'Saturday Night Palsy,' which muscle would you expect to be SPARED on needle EMG?
questions.explanation: Branches to triceps arise before the spiral groove. In spiral groove lesions, triceps is spared while muscles innervated distal to the groove (brachioradialis, extensors) are affected.

questions.question: The accessory deep peroneal nerve, when present, is confirmed by stimulating:
questions.explanation: The accessory deep peroneal nerve courses posterior to the lateral malleolus. Stimulating there while recording from EDB produces a CMAP that accounts for the amplitude difference between distal and proximal stimulation.

questions.question: In CNS disorders (e.g., stroke, spinal cord lesion), needle EMG typically shows:
choices: Reduced recruitment with normal MUAP morphology
questions.explanation: CNS disorders show reduced activation (a central process — reduced firing rate) with a normal recruitment pattern and normal MUAP morphology. Activation is a central process, while recruitment is peripheral.

questions.question: A patient cannot make an 'OK' sign with their thumb and index finger. They have weakness of FPL, FDP to digits 2-3, and pronator quadratus, but normal median sensory studies. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: AIN is a pure motor branch. The inability to make an 'OK' sign (making a triangle instead) is pathognomonic. Normal sensory studies exclude both CTS and pronator syndrome.

questions.question: The lumbrical-interosseous comparison study is useful for diagnosing:
questions.explanation: The 2nd lumbrical (median) vs 1st interosseous (ulnar) comparison uses the same distal distance, eliminating distance measurement as a variable. A latency difference greater than 0.5ms supports CTS.

questions.question: What is the upper limit of normal for the median motor distal latency according to the normative values table?
questions.explanation: The normative value for median motor distal latency (recording from APB, 8cm distance) is 4.5ms. This is one of the bolded/commonly performed studies in the competency curriculum.

questions.question: Which of the following motor NCS has the LARGEST normal amplitude?
questions.explanation: The ulnar motor study recording from ADM has the largest normal amplitude of the core studies at 6.0 mV. The peroneal motor study has the smallest at only 1.3 mV.

questions.question: The normal upper limit for the tibial F-wave latency is:
questions.explanation: The tibial F-wave has an upper limit of normal latency of 64.5ms. For patients taller than 180cm, this extends to 70.4ms. The acceptable side-to-side difference is 5.7ms.

questions.question: The upper limit of normal for the H-wave (tibial/soleus) latency is:
questions.explanation: The H-wave recorded from the tibial nerve/soleus has an upper limit of normal of 35.0ms, with a side-to-side difference threshold of 2.0ms.

questions.question: What is the appropriate gain setting for sensory NCS?
questions.explanation: Sensory NCS uses a gain of 20 microvolts/div with filters set at 10 (or 20) Hz to 2 kHz. Motor NCS uses 5 mV/div with 10 Hz to 10 kHz filters.

questions.question: During resting needle EMG, what gain setting should be used to detect spontaneous activity?
questions.explanation: Resting EMG uses 50 microvolts/div with filters at 20 Hz to 10 kHz, which is sensitive enough to detect small fibrillation potentials and PSWs. Recruitment EMG increases to 100-200 microvolts/div.

questions.question: Which of the following EMG potentials is classified as PRE-junctional?
questions.explanation: Fasciculation potentials originate pre-junctionally (in the nerve/motor neuron), along with myokymia and neuromyotonic discharges. Fibrillations, PSWs, CRDs, and myotonia are post-junctional (originating in the muscle fiber).

questions.question: Neuromyotonic discharges are characterized by which sound and are associated with which syndrome?
questions.explanation: Neuromyotonic discharges sound like Indy racing cars and are associated with Isaac's syndrome (neuromyotonia). They are pre-junctional and have a characteristic tornado appearance on the EMG screen.

questions.question: Myokymia on EMG is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Myokymia (bursting, marching soldiers sound, pre-junctional) is a key finding in radiation-induced neuropathy/plexopathy. Facial myokymia specifically points to a brainstem lesion (e.g., MS, brainstem glioma).

questions.question: The mnemonic for median nerve entrapment sites from proximal to distal is:
questions.explanation: Lig PAC stands for: Ligament of Struthers (rare, at distal humerus), Pronator Teres Syndrome, AIN Syndrome (pure motor), and CTS (carpal tunnel syndrome, at the wrist).

questions.question: In the palmar mixed nerve comparison technique for CTS, a latency difference of how many milliseconds between median and ulnar is considered abnormal?
questions.explanation: The palmar mixed nerve comparison (median vs ulnar, 8cm distance) uses a threshold of 0.4ms or greater, which is more sensitive than the ring finger comparison (which uses 0.5ms at 14cm).

questions.question: A patient with PIN syndrome has wrist drop. On examination, the wrist deviates radially on attempted extension. Why?
choices: The ECRL is paralyzed while ECU is spared
The ECRL is spared (innervated proximal to the Arcade of Frohse) while the ECU is paralyzed
The brachioradialis is the only functional wrist extensor
Radial deviation occurs because of unopposed median nerve function
questions.explanation: In PIN syndrome, the lesion is at the Arcade of Frohse. The ECRL (and brachioradialis, supinator) are innervated proximal to the arcade and therefore spared. The ECU and ECRB are innervated distal to it and are paralyzed. With only the ECRL functioning, wrist extension produces radial deviation. There is no sensory loss (PIN is pure motor).

questions.question: Martin-Gruber anastomosis is present in what percentage of the population, and what NCS findings does it create?
choices: 5%; increased distal CMAP on median studies
15-20%; decreased amplitude proximally on ulnar (false conduction block) and increased amplitude proximally on median
50%; bilateral slowing of ulnar CV across the elbow
28%; higher proximal than distal peroneal CMAP
questions.explanation: Martin-Gruber anastomosis (15-20% prevalence) is a median-to-ulnar motor fiber crossover in the forearm. It creates a false conduction block appearance on ulnar studies (decreased proximal amplitude), increased proximal amplitude on median studies, and an initial positive dip with proximal median stimulation recording hypothenar. Must be distinguished from true ulnar neuropathy.

questions.question: Which NMJ disorder is unique in producing fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves?
