questions.explanation: Botulism is the only NMJ disorder that produces fibrillation potentials and PSWs on needle EMG. Both MG and LEMS typically do not show fibrillations. Botulism is also pre-synaptic (like LEMS) and produces small CMAPs with facilitation, but the presence of denervation potentials differentiates it.

questions.question: Which single-fiber EMG measurement assesses jitter, and what percentage of pairs must be abnormal to call the study abnormal?
choices: Mean consecutive difference (MCD); greater than 10% of pairs (2 or more of 20)
questions.explanation: SFEMG jitter is measured as the mean consecutive difference (MCD) between two time-locked potentials from the same motor unit. The study is abnormal if more than 10% of pairs (2 or more out of 20 collected) exceed the upper limit of normal jitter for the muscle being tested and the patient's age.

questions.question: In the workup of polyneuropathy, which laboratory tests have the highest yield (Class III evidence)?
choices: CBC, ESR/CRP, B12, fasting glucose, thyroid function, serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis
questions.explanation: The basic laboratory investigation for polyneuropathy includes: CBC, ESR or CRP, vitamin B12 (with methylmalonic acid for borderline values), comprehensive metabolic panel (fasting glucose, renal/liver function), thyroid function, serum protein immunofixation electrophoresis, and glucose tolerance test if impaired glucose tolerance is suspected. Urine studies and drug/toxin history complete the workup.

questions.question: The normal latency range for the Sympathetic Skin Response (SSR) is:
questions.explanation: SSR has a normal latency of 1000-1500ms, reflecting the very slow unmyelinated sympathetic fibers. The low frequency filter is set extremely low (0.5 Hz). SSR is abnormal only when the response is entirely absent; its sensitivity is low.

questions.question: Standard NCS assess which type of nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: Standard NCS only test large, fast-conducting myelinated fibers. Small fiber neuropathies (pain, temperature, autonomic dysfunction) can have completely normal NCS. Small fiber testing requires specialized methods: skin biopsy (intraepidermal nerve fiber density), QSART, SSR, or autonomic testing.

questions.question: A patient presents with progressive proximal and distal weakness over 8 weeks with areflexia. NCS shows patchy demyelination with conduction block. CSF protein is elevated. This is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: CIDP (chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) is defined by progression over more than 8 weeks (distinguishing it from AIDP which peaks within 4 weeks). CIDP shows patchy, non-uniform demyelination with conduction block (unlike hereditary CMT1 which shows uniform slowing), elevated CSF protein, and responds to immunotherapy.

questions.question: In ALS, the El Escorial criteria require evidence of both upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in how many body regions for a 'definite' diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The El Escorial criteria for definite ALS require clinical evidence of both upper motor neuron (UMN) and lower motor neuron (LMN) signs in at least three of four body regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral). 'Probable' ALS requires UMN and LMN signs in two regions, with UMN signs rostral to LMN signs. EMG is key for demonstrating LMN involvement.

questions.question: 'Split hand syndrome' in ALS refers to:
choices: Weakness of FDS relative to FDP
Preferential wasting of thenar (APB) and first dorsal interosseous muscles relative to hypothenar muscles
Ulnar vs median nerve distribution weakness
Differential involvement of flexors vs extensors
questions.explanation: Split hand syndrome in ALS describes the preferential wasting and weakness of the lateral hand muscles (thenar eminence/APB and first dorsal interosseous) with relative preservation of the medial hand muscles (hypothenar/ADM). This pattern is relatively specific to ALS and helps distinguish it from other causes of hand weakness.

questions.question: Steroid myopathy typically shows which EMG/NCS pattern?
choices: Small, short, polyphasic MUAPs with fibrillations
Normal or abnormal EMG/NCS findings (may be normal)
questions.explanation: Steroid myopathy typically has normal or abnormal EMG/NCS findings - importantly, it may be entirely normal. Steroid myopathies preferentially affect type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers, but EMG recruitment evaluation primarily assesses type I fibers, which is why EMG can be misleadingly normal.

questions.question: In myotonic dystrophy, the characteristic EMG finding is:
choices: Myotonic discharges (waxing and waning in amplitude AND frequency)
questions.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy produces myotonic discharges - spontaneous potentials that characteristically wax and wane in BOTH amplitude and frequency, producing the classic 'dive bomber' or 'revving motorcycle' sound. This is distinct from CRDs which have abrupt onset/offset with NO wax/wane.

questions.question: When performing cardiovascular autonomic testing with deep breathing, the magnitude of heart rate change is most affected by:
questions.explanation: The magnitude of heart rate change with deep breathing is most affected by age. Heart rate normally increases with inspiration and decreases with expiration (sinus arrhythmia), but this response diminishes with advancing age, which must be accounted for when interpreting results.

questions.question: Safety considerations for EMG in patients with pacemakers/central lines include concern about:
choices: Electrical interference causing false positive results only
Risk of current traveling along the needle/lead causing cardiac arrhythmia
Risk of overheating the needle electrode
questions.explanation: In patients with pacemakers or central lines, the main safety concern is that electrical current from the stimulator could potentially travel along the needle or central line to the heart, potentially causing arrhythmia. Extra caution is needed with electrical stimulation near central lines and cardiac devices.

questions.question: The upper limit of normal for the peroneal motor distal latency is:
questions.explanation: The peroneal motor study (recording from EDB, ankle stimulation at 8cm) has an upper limit of normal distal latency of 6.5ms. The normal amplitude is only 1.3 mV - the lowest of the commonly performed motor studies, making it susceptible to technical factors.

questions.question: Which sensory nerve study has the SMALLEST normal amplitude?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve has the smallest normal amplitude at only 2 microvolts. Among the commonly performed (bolded) sensory studies, the sural nerve has the smallest at 4 microvolts. The median antidromic has 10 microvolts and ulnar antidromic has 6 microvolts.

questions.question: For patients taller than 180cm, what is the upper limit of normal for the median F-wave?
questions.explanation: For patients taller than 180cm, the median F-wave upper limit increases from 31.4ms to 34.2ms. The acceptable side-to-side difference is 2.2ms. Height correction is important because F-waves traverse the full length of the limb twice.

questions.question: The NMJ electrodiagnostic evaluation should follow what order?
choices: SFEMG first, then RNS, then routine NCS
Routine NCS, then RNS (3Hz supramaximal), then needle EMG, then SFEMG
RNS at 50Hz first, then sensory studies
questions.explanation: The recommended order for NMJ evaluation is: 1) Routine NCS (to assess CMAP amplitude and rule out other conditions), 2) RNS at 3Hz with supramaximal stimulation, 3) Needle EMG (to look for unstable MUAPs), 4) SFEMG (most sensitive test, done last). This stepwise approach goes from least to most sensitive.

questions.question: Which condition is an important differential diagnosis for ALS that must be excluded because it is treatable?
choices: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMNCB)
questions.explanation: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMNCB) is a crucial differential for ALS because it is treatable with IVIg. It presents with progressive asymmetric distal weakness, predominantly in upper extremities, with motor conduction block on NCS but no sensory abnormalities. Unlike ALS, there are no upper motor neuron signs.

questions.question: The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) has dual innervation. Which nerve supplies FDP to digits 4 and 5?
questions.explanation: FDP has dual innervation: the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN, branch of median) supplies FDP to digits 2-3, while the ulnar nerve supplies FDP to digits 4-5. This dual innervation is a high-yield exam topic and clinically important for localizing lesions.

questions.question: A patient presents with inability to flex the DIP joints of digits 2 and 3, inability to flex the IP joint of the thumb, and weakness of forearm pronation. Sensation is preserved. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve. It innervates FPL (thumb IP flexion), FDP to digits 2-3 (DIP flexion), and pronator quadratus (deep pronation). It has NO sensory component, so sensation is preserved. Loss of the 'OK sign' (pinch between thumb and index) is the classic test.

questions.question: Which classic hand deformity results from median nerve injury at the ELBOW level?
questions.explanation: Median nerve injury at the elbow causes 'Hand of Benediction' — when attempting to make a fist, digits 1 and 2 remain extended because FDS and FDP (to digits 2-3) are paralyzed. At the WRIST level (e.g., CTS), the result is 'Ape Hand' with thenar wasting and loss of thumb opposition.

questions.question: A patient has wrist drop with inability to extend the wrist and fingers, but triceps function is PRESERVED. Where is the radial nerve lesion?
questions.explanation: Spiral groove lesion spares the triceps (innervated proximal to the spiral groove) but affects brachioradialis and all distal extensors, producing wrist drop with preserved elbow extension. If triceps were also weak, the lesion would be at the axilla level. PIN lesion produces finger drop without wrist drop (ECRL spared).

questions.question: What is the brachial plexus mnemonic 'Risk Takers Don't Cautiously Behave' for?
choices: The order of structures: Roots, Trunks, Divisions, Cords, Branches
The three cords: lateral, posterior, medial
questions.explanation: 'Risk Takers Don't Cautiously Behave' = Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches. This represents the five organizational levels of the brachial plexus from proximal (spinal roots C5-T1) to distal (terminal branches like median, ulnar, radial, musculocutaneous, axillary).

questions.question: The median nerve arises from which cord(s) of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The median nerve is unique — it has TWO heads (roots): a lateral head from the lateral cord and a medial head from the medial cord. They join anterior to the axillary artery to form the median nerve. This dual origin is frequently tested.

questions.question: Which terminal branch arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The posterior cord gives rise to the axillary nerve and the radial nerve. The lateral cord gives musculocutaneous and the lateral head of median. The medial cord gives ulnar, medial head of median, and the medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm.

questions.question: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is clinically important because it runs adjacent to which vein?
questions.explanation: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve runs adjacent to the basilic vein in the medial arm and forearm. This makes it vulnerable to injury during venipuncture, IV access, or PICC line placement at the antecubital fossa. Injury causes numbness along the medial forearm.

questions.question: In the superficial layer of the anterior forearm, which muscle is the ONLY one innervated by the ulnar nerve?
questions.explanation: FCU is the only superficial anterior forearm muscle innervated by the ulnar nerve (C7-T1). All other superficial muscles (pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus) are median-innervated. FCU flexes and adducts (ulnar deviates) the wrist. It is the first ulnar-innervated forearm muscle tested in suspected cubital tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: For EMG needle electrode insertion into the biceps brachii, the recommended depth is approximately:
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii requires 3-6 Units/kg depth for EMG needle insertion. This is among the deepest forearm/arm muscles. By comparison, pronator quadratus is the shallowest at 0.5-1 Units/kg, and pronator teres is 1-2 Units/kg. Knowledge of appropriate needle depth helps avoid injury to deeper structures.

questions.question: Cutaneous innervation of the lateral forearm is provided by which nerve?
choices: Musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm)
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve becomes the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm after piercing the deep fascia lateral to the biceps tendon. It provides sensation to the lateral forearm. This is important because the lateral antebrachial cutaneous (LABC) sensory nerve study tests the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.question: Which nerve injury causes 'winged scapula' due to serratus anterior weakness?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) innervates the serratus anterior. Injury causes the medial border of the scapula to protrude posteriorly (winged scapula), especially when pushing against a wall. Causes include surgery (axillary lymph node dissection), heavy backpack use, and viral neuritis (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).

questions.question: Erb-Duchenne palsy involves which brachial plexus component?
questions.explanation: Erb-Duchenne palsy is an upper trunk (C5-C6) injury producing the classic 'waiter's tip' position — the arm hangs at the side, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated. Shoulder abduction (deltoid), external rotation (infraspinatus), and elbow flexion (biceps) are lost. Common from birth trauma or falls on the shoulder.

questions.question: The 'ulnar paradox' refers to the finding that claw hand deformity is:
choices: Worse with distal ulnar lesions (at wrist)
Equal at all levels of injury
Only present with combined median-ulnar lesions
questions.explanation: The ulnar paradox: claw hand is MORE pronounced with DISTAL (wrist) ulnar lesions. With proximal lesions (elbow), FDP to digits 4-5 is also paralyzed, so the DIP joints cannot flex into the 'claw' position. With distal lesions, FDP function is preserved (innervated above the lesion), allowing the unopposed clawing of the ring and small fingers.

questions.question: Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) syndrome differs from radial nerve palsy at the spiral groove in that PIN syndrome:
choices: Causes sensory loss on the dorsal hand
Causes finger drop WITHOUT wrist drop
questions.explanation: PIN is a pure motor branch. PIN syndrome causes finger/thumb extension weakness WITHOUT wrist drop because the ECRL (innervated before the PIN takeoff) is spared, allowing wrist extension. There is no sensory loss (unlike spiral groove lesion which affects the superficial radial sensory branch). The wrist may deviate radially on extension.

questions.question: In carpal tunnel syndrome, which two physical examination tests are most commonly used?
questions.explanation: Phalen maneuver (sustained wrist flexion for 60 seconds reproduces paresthesias in the median nerve distribution) and Tinel sign (percussion over the carpal tunnel at the wrist produces tingling in the median nerve distribution) are the classic CTS provocative tests. Froment and Wartenberg signs test ulnar nerve function.

questions.question: Axillary nerve injury typically results from anterior shoulder dislocation. The sensory loss is in the:
questions.explanation: Axillary nerve injury causes sensory loss in the 'regimental badge area' — a patch over the lateral deltoid/shoulder region, supplied by the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (terminal sensory branch of axillary nerve). Motor loss affects deltoid (shoulder abduction) and teres minor (external rotation).

questions.question: At the wrist, the tendon landmarks from RADIAL to ULNAR are:
questions.explanation: From radial to ulnar at the wrist: FCR (flexor carpi radialis) → PL (palmaris longus) → FCU (flexor carpi ulnaris). The median nerve lies between FCR and PL (or deep to PL). Palmaris longus is absent in ~15% of people. These landmarks are essential for locating structures during NCS and injection procedures.

questions.question: The sensory territory of the posterior forearm and posterior arm is supplied primarily by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve dominates the posterior upper extremity sensory supply: posterior cutaneous nerve of arm (posterior arm), posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm (posterior forearm), and superficial branch of radial nerve (dorsal hand/first web space). Anteriorly, cutaneous supply transitions from axillary (shoulder) → radial (lateral arm) → musculocutaneous (lateral forearm) → median (hand).

questions.question: In the deep anterior forearm compartment, pronator quadratus has the SHALLOWEST EMG insertion depth at:
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus (AIN branch of median, C8-T1) has the shallowest EMG insertion depth at 0.5-1 Units/kg despite being a 'deep' compartment muscle — this is because it lies directly on the interosseous membrane of the distal forearm with relatively little overlying tissue when accessed from the volar surface. Compare with biceps/brachialis at 3-6 Units/kg.

questions.question: For the median motor NCS recording from APB, the E1 (active) electrode is placed:
choices: Over the most prominent part of the thenar eminence, midway between wrist crease and 1st MCP
Over the adductor pollicis in the first web space
Over the flexor pollicis brevis at the wrist
questions.explanation: The E1 active electrode is placed over the motor point of the APB muscle — at the most prominent part of the thenar eminence, approximately midway between the midpoint of the wrist crease and the 1st MCP joint. The E2 reference goes on the proximal phalanx of the thumb or 1st MCP joint.

questions.question: What does an initial POSITIVE deflection on a motor NCS CMAP indicate?
choices: The E1 electrode is OFF the motor point — needs repositioning
questions.explanation: An initial positive (downward) deflection means the E1 (active) electrode is not directly over the motor point. The action potential is approaching E1 from a distance rather than starting under it. Solution: reposition E1 toward the muscle belly until you get a clean negative (upward) initial deflection. This applies to ALL motor NCS studies.

questions.question: The standard distal distance for ALL four core motor studies (median, ulnar, peroneal, tibial) is:
questions.explanation: All four core motor NCS studies use a standardized 8 cm distance from the distal stimulation site to the E1 recording electrode. This is critical — changing the distance changes the distal latency calculation. For sensory studies, the standard distance is 14 cm (wrist to digit for upper extremity; calf to malleolus for sural).

questions.question: During ulnar motor NCS, the elbow should be positioned at:
questions.explanation: The elbow MUST be flexed to 70-90° for accurate across-elbow ulnar motor NCS. With extension, the ulnar nerve follows a shorter path through the ulnar groove — measuring surface distance overestimates the actual nerve path length, producing falsely slow conduction velocities across the elbow.

questions.question: Which of the four core motor studies has the LOWEST normal amplitude?
questions.explanation: The peroneal motor study recording from EDB has the lowest normal amplitude at only 1.3 mV. This makes it particularly susceptible to technical factors and normal aging (EDB atrophy). In some patients, recording from tibialis anterior may give better results. The ulnar motor has the highest normal amplitude at 6.0 mV.

questions.question: Martin-Gruber anastomosis is present in approximately what percentage of patients?
questions.explanation: Martin-Gruber anastomosis (median-to-ulnar crossover in the forearm) occurs in 15-20% of the population. It can cause: (1) larger CMAP with elbow than wrist stimulation on median motor, (2) larger CMAP with above-elbow than below-elbow on ulnar motor, (3) false appearance of conduction block. Recognition prevents misdiagnosis.

questions.question: The tibial motor CMAP amplitude normally drops 21-50% between ankle and popliteal fossa stimulation. This should NOT be misinterpreted as:
questions.explanation: A normal physiological amplitude drop of 21-50% occurs between ankle and popliteal fossa in tibial motor studies due to phase cancellation over the long nerve segment. This is NOT conduction block. True conduction block requires >50% amplitude drop with <15% temporal dispersion. Recognizing this normal finding prevents unnecessary workup for conduction block.

questions.question: When performing peroneal motor NCS, if the ankle CMAP is SMALLER than the below-fibular-head CMAP, you should suspect:
questions.explanation: If ankle amplitude is smaller than proximal amplitude, suspect an accessory peroneal nerve — a branch from the superficial peroneal nerve that courses BEHIND the lateral malleolus to innervate lateral portions of EDB. Confirm by stimulating behind the lateral malleolus — you'll get a CMAP that, added to the ankle CMAP, equals the proximal CMAP.

questions.question: For the sural sensory NCS, the E1 recording electrode is placed:
choices: On the dorsum of the foot
On the lateral border of the foot
questions.explanation: The sural sensory E1 is placed posterior to (behind) the lateral malleolus. The stimulation site is on the posterolateral calf, 14 cm proximal to E1. The sural nerve runs along the posterolateral calf between the two heads of the gastrocnemius. Patient positioning: prone or lateral decubitus with the recording leg up.

questions.question: A sural sensory response is expected to be NORMAL in:
questions.explanation: The sural sensory is NORMAL in radiculopathy because the lesion is pre-ganglionic (proximal to the dorsal root ganglion). The DRG and its peripheral sensory axons remain intact, so the sural SNAP is preserved. This is a fundamental principle: sensory responses are normal in radiculopathy but abnormal in plexopathy and peripheral nerve lesions.

questions.question: For the median motor NCS, the wrist stimulation site is located between which two tendons?
questions.explanation: The median nerve at the wrist lies between the FCR (flexor carpi radialis) and palmaris longus tendons. The cathode is placed here, 8 cm proximal to E1 on APB, at the proximal wrist crease. Remember the radial-to-ulnar tendon landmarks: FCR → PL → FCU. The median nerve travels between the first two.

questions.question: What is the minimum across-elbow distance required for accurate ulnar motor conduction velocity measurement?
questions.explanation: The across-elbow distance (above-elbow to below-elbow stimulation sites) must be at least 10 cm, measured along the ulnar groove with the elbow flexed at 70-90°. Shorter distances magnify measurement errors — a 1 cm error in a 10 cm segment causes 10% CV error, but the same error in a 5 cm segment causes 20% error.

questions.question: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous (DUC) sensory nerve branches from the ulnar nerve:
choices: At the wrist in Guyon's canal
questions.explanation: The DUC branches 5-8 cm proximal to the wrist. This is clinically crucial: DUC is SPARED in both cubital tunnel syndrome (lesion at elbow, above the DUC branch) — wait, actually DUC would be affected in cubital tunnel since the lesion is proximal. The DUC is SPARED in Guyon's canal lesions (distal to the branching point). An abnormal DUC helps localize the ulnar lesion to the elbow or above.

questions.question: What minimum temperature must be maintained at the hand during upper extremity NCS?
questions.explanation: Hand temperature must be ≥32°C for accurate upper extremity NCS. For the leg, ≥30°C is required. Cold temperatures prolong distal latencies, slow conduction velocities, and INCREASE amplitudes (counterintuitive — cold slows Na+ channel inactivation, prolonging each action potential). Always warm the limb if temperature is below threshold.

questions.question: Supramaximal stimulation means increasing stimulus intensity above the maximal response by:
questions.explanation: Supramaximal stimulation = increase intensity 20-25% above the level that produces the maximal CMAP or SNAP amplitude. This ensures all nerve fibers are activated. Typical supramaximal motor NCS requires 15-20 mA at the wrist, with higher intensities needed at deeper sites (popliteal fossa, below fibular head). Never exceed 50 mA in children.

questions.question: For the CTS median vs ulnar comparison study to digit 4, a latency difference of ≥ ___ ms is considered abnormal:
questions.explanation: Median vs ulnar sensory comparison to digit 4: both nerves are stimulated at the same 14 cm distance at the wrist, with recording electrodes on digit 4. A peak latency difference ≥0.5 ms (median slower than ulnar) supports CTS. For the palmar mixed nerve comparison across the carpal tunnel, the threshold is ≥0.4 ms.

questions.question: The peroneal motor NCS requires stimulation at how many sites for a complete study?
choices: 4 (ankle, mid-leg, below fibular head, popliteal fossa)
questions.explanation: A complete peroneal motor study requires THREE stimulation sites: ankle, below fibular head (BFH), and popliteal fossa (or above fibular head). Skipping the BFH site risks missing fibular neck pathology — the most common site of peroneal nerve compression. The BFH site requires higher stimulation current because the nerve runs deep at that level.

questions.question: Which sensory NCS distance is standard for both upper AND lower extremity studies?
questions.explanation: 14 cm is the standard sensory NCS distance for both upper extremity (median wrist-to-digit, ulnar wrist-to-digit) and lower extremity (sural calf-to-malleolus) studies. Motor studies use 8 cm as their standard distal distance. The 7 cm midpalm distance is used for the palmar mixed nerve study across the carpal tunnel (half of the 14 cm wrist distance).

questions.question: On the ulnar motor NCS, an amplitude drop >20% between above-elbow and below-elbow stimulation with minimal temporal dispersion suggests:
questions.explanation: An amplitude drop >20% between AE and BE stimulation with <15% change in CMAP duration (temporal dispersion) strongly suggests conduction block at the elbow — the hallmark of ulnar neuropathy at the elbow (cubital tunnel syndrome). A conduction velocity drop below 43 m/s across the elbow is the other key finding. An inching study (1-2 cm increments) can precisely localize the block.

questions.question: The ground electrode in NCS should always be placed:
choices: Between the stimulating and recording electrodes
As far as possible from all other electrodes
questions.explanation: The ground electrode is ALWAYS placed between the stimulating and recording electrodes. This reduces stimulus artifact and electrical noise. Proper grounding is essential for clean recordings, especially for small sensory responses. The ground can be a surface electrode pad or a strap electrode placed on the dorsum of the hand or foot.

flashcards.front: Supraspinatus - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Suprascapular nerve, C5-C6

flashcards.front: Infraspinatus - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Suprascapular nerve, C5-C6

flashcards.front: Deltoid - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Axillary nerve, C5-C6

flashcards.front: Biceps brachii - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C6

flashcards.front: Triceps brachii - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Radial nerve, C6-C8

flashcards.front: Flexor carpi radialis - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Median nerve, C6-C7

flashcards.front: Flexor carpi ulnaris - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Ulnar nerve, C8-T1

flashcards.front: Abductor pollicis brevis - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Median nerve, C8-T1

flashcards.front: First dorsal interosseous - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Ulnar nerve, C8-T1

flashcards.front: Iliopsoas - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Femoral nerve (plus direct lumbar plexus branches), L1-L3

flashcards.front: Tibialis anterior - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Deep fibular (peroneal) nerve, L4-L5

flashcards.front: Gastrocnemius - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Tibial nerve, S1-S2

flashcards.front: Adductor longus - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Obturator nerve, L2-L4

flashcards.front: Gluteus medius - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Superior gluteal nerve, L4-S1

flashcards.front: Biceps femoris, short head - nerve and root?
flashcards.back: Fibular division of the sciatic nerve, L5-S2

flashcards.front: Initial deflection of a fibrillation potential?
flashcards.back: Initial POSITIVE deflection - biphasic/triphasic, duration under 5 ms, amplitude up to about 1 mV, fires regularly

flashcards.front: Initial deflection of an end-plate spike?
flashcards.back: Initial NEGATIVE deflection - duration 0.5 to 2 ms, amplitude 10 to 50 microvolts, fires irregularly, occurs only in the end-plate zone

flashcards.front: What distinguishes a CRD from a myotonic discharge?
flashcards.back: CRDs have abrupt onset/offset with no wax or wane and an unvarying repeating waveform (ephaptic transmission); myotonic discharges wax and wane in both amplitude and frequency

flashcards.front: Sound classically associated with positive sharp waves?
flashcards.back: A dull thud

flashcards.front: Sound classically associated with complex repetitive discharges?
flashcards.back: Machine gun

flashcards.front: Sound classically associated with myotonic discharges?
flashcards.back: Dive bomber, or a revving motorcycle

flashcards.front: Firing pattern of a fasciculation potential?
flashcards.back: Irregular, about 1 Hz to several times per minute; has motor-unit morphology; can be a normal or a pathologic finding

flashcards.front: What is myokymia on needle EMG?
flashcards.back: Grouped, repetitive discharges of the same motor unit(s) recurring in bursts at regular intervals (marching soldiers sound); seen in radiation plexopathy, MS, Guillain-Barre syndrome, facial myokymia

flashcards.front: What generates end-plate noise?
flashcards.back: Subthreshold miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs); low amplitude 10 to 40 microvolts, monophasic negative, seashell-roar sound; a normal end-plate zone finding

flashcards.front: Typical firing frequency of a cramp potential?
flashcards.back: High frequency, up to about 150 Hz; irregular, involuntary, painful motor unit discharges

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Formula for conduction velocity?
flashcards.back: Distance divided by time, using the latency DIFFERENCE between two stimulation sites, not the distal latency alone

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Why does SNAP amplitude reflect only large myelinated fibers?
flashcards.back: Slower fibers desynchronize over distance and their small individual contributions cancel out of the summated potential, leaving mainly the fast, large fibers to summate into the recordable peak

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: What side-to-side CMAP amplitude difference is considered abnormal?
flashcards.back: Greater than about 50 percent

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Optimal inter-electrode (G1 to G2) distance for sensory studies?
flashcards.back: About 3 to 4 cm

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Effect of moving G2 too close to G1?
flashcards.back: Decreased amplitude and a falsely shortened (earlier) peak latency, due to cancellation between the two electrodes

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Effect of increasing the low-frequency filter on amplitude and duration?
flashcards.back: Blunts (decreases) amplitude and decreases duration

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Recommended surface temperature for upper limb NCS?
flashcards.back: 32 degrees C

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Recommended surface temperature for lower limb NCS?
flashcards.back: 30 degrees C

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Effect of limb cooling on amplitude, duration, and conduction velocity?
flashcards.back: Increases amplitude, increases duration, decreases conduction velocity (and increases distal latency)

flashcards.category: NCS Normal Values and Technical Factors
flashcards.front: Approximate conduction velocity decrease per degree C of cooling below 32 degrees C (upper limb)?
flashcards.back: About 2.4 m/s per degree C

flashcards.front: Seddon classification - neurapraxia?
flashcards.back: Focal conduction block from myelin injury; axon intact; no Wallerian degeneration; best prognosis, recovery over days to weeks

flashcards.front: Seddon classification - axonotmesis?
flashcards.back: Axon disrupted with Wallerian degeneration; connective tissue framework (endoneurium) preserved; regeneration at about 1 mm per day; good but gradual recovery

flashcards.front: Seddon classification - neurotmesis?
flashcards.back: Complete disruption of the axon and all connective tissue layers; no spontaneous recovery; surgical repair usually required

flashcards.front: Sunderland degrees 2 through 4 all correspond to which Seddon category?
flashcards.back: Axonotmesis - they subdivide it by which connective tissue layers (endoneurium, perineurium) remain intact

flashcards.front: When does motor NCS become abnormal distal to an acute nerve transection?
flashcards.back: About day 3 to 5 post-injury, once Wallerian degeneration is far enough along

flashcards.front: When does sensory NCS become abnormal distal to an acute nerve transection?
flashcards.back: About day 6 to 10 post-injury

flashcards.front: Timeline for fibrillation potentials to appear after axon loss - proximal versus distal muscles?
flashcards.back: About 10 to 14 days in proximal muscles; about 3 to 4 weeks in distal muscles

flashcards.front: Earliest EMG finding after acute axonotmesis, before fibrillations appear?
flashcards.back: Reduced recruitment (fewer motor units available), with otherwise normal-appearing MUAP morphology

flashcards.front: Why are SNAPs normal in radiculopathy despite sensory symptoms?
flashcards.back: The lesion is proximal to (or at) the dorsal root ganglion, that is, preganglionic, so the sensory cell body and peripheral axon remain intact

flashcards.front: What EMG finding is the key to localizing a lesion to the nerve root, versus plexus or peripheral nerve?
flashcards.back: Paraspinal muscle denervation - abnormal in radiculopathy, spared in plexopathy and mononeuropathy

flashcards.front: SNAP status in plexopathy versus radiculopathy?
flashcards.back: Abnormal in plexopathy (postganglionic lesion); normal in radiculopathy (preganglionic lesion)

flashcards.front: How do you tell an old, inactive radiculopathy from an active one on needle EMG?
flashcards.back: Fibrillation potentials/PSWs indicate active denervation; chronic neurogenic MUAP changes (large, long-duration, polyphasic) without fibrillations indicate an old, stable lesion

flashcards.front: Which muscle differentiates an L5 radiculopathy from an isolated fibular neuropathy?
flashcards.back: Posterior tibialis (tibial nerve, L5) - abnormal in L5 radiculopathy, normal in fibular neuropathy

flashcards.front: Typical NMJ disorder localization pattern for SNAP, CMAP, and needle EMG?
flashcards.back: Normal SNAP; normal (or low in LEMS) CMAP; normal or mildly unstable MUAPs; no fibrillations typically

flashcards.front: Typical myopathy localization pattern for SNAP, NCV, MUAPs, and recruitment?
flashcards.back: Normal SNAP and NCV; small, short, polyphasic MUAPs; early/full recruitment

flashcards.front: Which three muscles help evaluate a foot drop to distinguish L5 radiculopathy from fibular neuropathy?
flashcards.back: Posterior tibialis, tensor fasciae latae, and lumbar paraspinal muscles

flashcards.front: C6 radiculopathy - which late response is characteristically abnormal?
flashcards.back: The flexor carpi radialis H-reflex, assessing C6-C7

flashcards.front: Sciatic neuropathy - which division is more vulnerable to injury?
flashcards.back: The fibular (peroneal) division, due to less connective tissue support and fewer fascicles than the tibial division

flashcards.front: Myasthenia gravis - presynaptic or postsynaptic, and antibody target?
flashcards.back: Postsynaptic; antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (or MuSK in a subset of patients)

flashcards.front: Myasthenia gravis - RNS finding and associated tumor?
flashcards.back: Greater than 10 percent decrement at 2-3 Hz repetitive stimulation; associated with thymoma

flashcards.front: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome - presynaptic or postsynaptic, and antibody target?
flashcards.back: Presynaptic; antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC)

flashcards.front: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome - RNS/exercise finding and associated malignancy?
flashcards.back: Greater than 100 percent increment after brief exercise or rapid RNS; associated with small cell lung cancer

flashcards.front: Botulism - mechanism and classic infantile presentation?
flashcards.back: Presynaptic blockade of acetylcholine vesicle release (SNARE protein cleavage); infantile botulism presents with constipation, hypotonia, and bulbar weakness

flashcards.front: What resting CMAP amplitude pattern distinguishes LEMS/botulism from myasthenia gravis?
flashcards.back: LEMS and botulism show LOW resting CMAP amplitude; myasthenia gravis typically shows a NORMAL resting CMAP amplitude

flashcards.front: Definition of the neuromuscular safety factor?
flashcards.back: The ratio of acetylcholine released per nerve impulse to the minimum amount needed to reach threshold for a muscle fiber action potential

flashcards.front: What mechanism is common to all NMJ disorders (MG, LEMS, botulism)?
flashcards.back: A reduced safety factor of neuromuscular transmission, regardless of whether the defect is presynaptic or postsynaptic

flashcards.front: F-wave - stimulus intensity and trial-to-trial consistency?
flashcards.back: Supramaximal stimulus; variable latency and morphology from trial to trial, due to antidromic motor neuron backfiring

flashcards.front: F-wave amplitude relative to the CMAP?
flashcards.back: About 1 to 5 percent of the CMAP amplitude

flashcards.front: H-reflex - stimulus intensity and trial-to-trial consistency?
flashcards.back: Submaximal stimulus; stable, reproducible latency and amplitude (a true monosynaptic reflex arc)

flashcards.front: Most common H-reflex sites and the roots they assess?
flashcards.back: Tibial nerve/soleus (assesses S1) and median nerve/flexor carpi radialis (assesses C6-C7)

flashcards.front: A-wave (axon reflex) - key identifying feature?
flashcards.back: Constant latency and morphology on every trial, typically appearing between the M-wave and F-wave, best seen at moderate (submaximal) stimulus intensities

flashcards.front: Blink reflex R1 versus R2 pathway?
flashcards.back: R1 = early, ipsilateral, oligosynaptic (trigeminal to pons to facial nerve); R2 = later, bilateral, polysynaptic (trigeminal to medulla to bilateral facial nerve nuclei)

flashcards.front: Most sensitive NCS segment for early/mild carpal tunnel syndrome, and its main limitation?
flashcards.back: The median wrist-to-palm short segment; its short distance magnifies the effect of measurement error

flashcards.front: Why is dorsal hand sensation spared in a Guyon's canal (wrist) ulnar lesion but not in a more proximal ulnar lesion?
flashcards.back: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist, about 5 to 8 cm proximal to the ulnar styloid, before Guyon's canal

flashcards.front: Froment's sign indicates weakness of which muscle and nerve?
flashcards.back: Adductor pollicis, innervated by the ulnar nerve

flashcards.front: Handlebar palsy - nerve and site?
flashcards.back: Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal (wrist), from prolonged handlebar pressure

flashcards.front: Most common site of fibular (peroneal) nerve entrapment?
flashcards.back: The fibular head

flashcards.front: Tarsal tunnel syndrome - nerve and location?
flashcards.back: Tibial nerve, entrapped behind the medial malleolus at the flexor retinaculum

flashcards.front: True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome affects which part of the brachial plexus?
flashcards.back: The lower trunk (C8-T1)

flashcards.front: Suprascapular nerve entrapment at the spinoglenoid notch versus the suprascapular notch?
flashcards.back: Spinoglenoid notch affects infraspinatus only; suprascapular notch affects both supraspinatus and infraspinatus

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus - which cord gives rise to the axillary and radial nerves?
flashcards.back: The posterior cord

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus - which cord gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve?
flashcards.back: The lateral cord

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus - which cord gives rise to the ulnar nerve?
flashcards.back: The medial cord

flashcards.front: Sciatic nerve - root levels and its two divisions?
flashcards.back: L4-S3; composed of the tibial (medial) and fibular/peroneal (lateral) divisions

flashcards.front: Femoral nerve position relative to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle?
flashcards.back: Immediately lateral to the femoral artery (mnemonic NAVEL: Nerve-Artery-Vein-Empty space-Lymphatics, lateral to medial)

flashcards.front: What is the normal MUAP duration range?
flashcards.back: 5-15ms. Duration is the most important MUAP parameter and reflects total muscle fiber count in the motor unit.

flashcards.front: MUAP amplitude reflects how many fibers?
flashcards.back: Only the 2-12 muscle fibers closest to the recording electrode (a high-frequency component filtered by tissue).

flashcards.front: What rise time indicates the needle is properly positioned?
flashcards.back: Less than 500 microseconds. If rise time exceeds this, reposition the needle before analyzing MUAP parameters.

flashcards.front: How do nascent motor units differ from myopathic MUAPs?
flashcards.back: Both are short, small, polyphasic — but nascent units have REDUCED recruitment while myopathic units have early/normal recruitment.

flashcards.front: What percentage of deltoid MUAPs can normally be polyphasic?
flashcards.back: Up to 25% (an exception to the general 10% rule used for other muscles).

flashcards.front: What is the size principle?
flashcards.back: Small motor neurons (Type I, slow-twitch) are recruited first; large motor neurons (Type II, fast-twitch) are recruited only with maximal contraction.

flashcards.front: What does activation vs recruitment mean?
flashcards.back: Activation = central process (firing rate of individual motor units); Recruitment = peripheral process (adding new motor units). CNS disorders reduce activation; peripheral disorders reduce recruitment.

flashcards.front: What MUAP pattern is seen in chronic neuropathic conditions?
flashcards.back: Large, long-duration, polyphasic MUAPs with DECREASED recruitment (reinnervation increases motor unit territory).

flashcards.front: What is the elbow position for ulnar motor NCS?
flashcards.back: Flexed at 70-90 degrees — more sensitive than extended for detecting ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.

flashcards.front: Name the 5 types of Guyon's canal syndrome.
flashcards.back: Type 1 = combined motor+sensory; Type 2 = pure sensory; Type 3 = deep palmar + hypothenar motor; Type 4 = deep palmar motor only (spares hypothenar); Type 5 = distal deep palmar motor only.

flashcards.front: Why is the dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch important for localization?
flashcards.back: It arises proximal to the wrist — spared in Guyon's canal lesions, abnormal in elbow lesions. Helps differentiate the entrapment site.

flashcards.front: What is the FDIH advantage over ADM for ulnar studies?
flashcards.back: FDIH (first dorsal interosseous-hypothenar) may be more sensitive than ADM for detecting ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.

flashcards.front: What is the most common site of radial nerve injury?
flashcards.back: The spiral groove — 'Saturday Night Palsy,' from compression during deep sleep or intoxication.

flashcards.front: What differentiates a PIN lesion from spiral groove radial neuropathy?
flashcards.back: PIN = wrist drop with radial deviation (ECRL spared), no sensory loss; spiral groove = wrist drop without deviation, decreased superficial radial sensory response.

flashcards.front: What EDX findings distinguish radial neuropathy by level?
flashcards.back: PIN: normal sensory, motor abnormalities distally. Spiral groove: low sensory + motor, triceps spared. Axilla: same as spiral groove plus triceps involved.

flashcards.front: Where is the recording electrode for tibial motor NCS?
flashcards.back: Abductor hallucis (AH) — medial foot, two finger widths distal to the navicular bone, belly-tendon method.

flashcards.front: What nerve is the 'gold standard' sensory study in the lower extremity?
flashcards.back: The sural nerve. G1 posterior to the lateral malleolus, stimulate midcalf at 14cm.

flashcards.front: Name the key tibial-innervated muscles and their root levels.
flashcards.back: Medial gastrocnemius (S1-S2), lateral gastrocnemius (L5-S1-S2), soleus (S1-S2), tibialis posterior (L5-S1), FHL (L5-S1-S2), FDL (L5-S1-S2).

flashcards.front: What localizes a peroneal neuropathy vs a sciatic lesion?
flashcards.back: The short head of biceps femoris — the only muscle above the knee innervated by the peroneal division. Normal = fibular head; abnormal = sciatic or higher.

flashcards.front: What does a normal superficial peroneal sensory study plus complete foot drop suggest?
flashcards.back: A demyelinating conduction block at the fibular head — axons are intact (sensory normal) but motor conduction is blocked.

flashcards.front: What is the accessory deep peroneal nerve?
flashcards.back: Present in about 28% of people; supplies the lateral EDB via a branch posterior to the lateral malleolus. Causes a higher proximal than distal CMAP amplitude (don't confuse with conduction block).

flashcards.front: What are the median motor NCS recording sites?
flashcards.back: Active (G1) over the APB (one-third of the distance between the metacarpal-carpal crease and MCP joint), reference (G2) on the MCP joint 4-5cm distal, ground on the back of the hand.

flashcards.front: What are the sensory latency and motor latency cutoffs for CTS?
flashcards.back: Sensory greater than 4.0ms (digital); motor distal latency greater than 4.4ms.

flashcards.front: What is the ring finger comparison technique for CTS?
flashcards.back: Compare median and ulnar antidromic sensory latencies from the 4th digit. A difference greater than 0.5ms is abnormal (supports CTS).

flashcards.front: Name the 4 median nerve entrapment sites, distal to proximal.
flashcards.back: 1) Carpal tunnel (wrist), 2) Pronator syndrome (between the heads of pronator teres), 3) AIN syndrome (forearm), 4) Ligament of Struthers (elbow — rare).

flashcards.front: What is the pathognomonic sign of AIN syndrome?
flashcards.back: Cannot make an 'OK' sign — makes a triangle instead (FPL, FDP to digits 2-3, and PQ weakness). Pure motor — sensory studies are normal.

flashcards.front: What are the five branches of the facial nerve?
flashcards.back: Temporal (frontalis), zygomatic (orbicularis oculi), buccal (nasalis/orbicularis oris), marginal mandibular (mentalis), cervical (platysma).

flashcards.front: What are the normal blink reflex latencies?
flashcards.back: R1 = 8-13ms (ipsilateral only); R2 = 28-42ms (ipsilateral); R2c = 29-44ms (contralateral).

flashcards.front: What is the blink reflex arc?
flashcards.back: Afferent = trigeminal nerve (CN V, supraorbital branch); efferent = facial nerve (CN VII). R1 = disynaptic (ipsilateral), R2 = polysynaptic (bilateral).

flashcards.front: What is the earliest detectable EDX abnormality in GBS?
flashcards.back: Blink reflex abnormalities (or absent/prolonged F-waves). The blink reflex may be more sensitive than standard NCS early in the disease course.

flashcards.front: What defines conduction block on NCS?
flashcards.back: A drop of at least 50% in CMAP area or amplitude between distal and proximal stimulation. It does NOT occur with pure axonal loss — it is a sign of demyelination.

flashcards.front: What is the 'sural sparing pattern'?
flashcards.back: Preserved sural SNAP with abnormal median/ulnar sensory responses. Characteristic of CIDP (an acquired demyelinating neuropathy).

flashcards.front: What is the CV calculation formula, with an example?
flashcards.back: CV = distance / time. Example: 250mm between two stimulation points, latency difference 4.5ms, so CV = 250/4.5 = 55.6 m/s.

flashcards.front: What are the limitations of standard NCS?
flashcards.back: They only test large myelinated fibers. Small fiber neuropathies (pain, temperature, autonomic) can have completely normal NCS.

flashcards.front: How does the F-wave differ from the H-reflex?
flashcards.back: F-wave = supramaximal, variable latency/morphology, 1-5% of motor neurons backfire. H-reflex = submaximal, stable latency, a true monosynaptic reflex.

flashcards.front: What interference pattern is seen with CNS lesions?
flashcards.back: Reduced activation (decreased firing rate — a central problem) with normal MUAP morphology and normal recruitment ratio. Compare to neuropathic: reduced recruitment with increased firing rate.

flashcards.front: What muscles does the median nerve's AIN branch supply?
flashcards.back: FPL (flexor pollicis longus), FDP to digits 2-3, and pronator quadratus. Pure motor — no sensory component.

flashcards.front: When is CTS most severe on EMG?
flashcards.back: When there is atrophy, chronic denervation, absent sensory responses, and prolonged/absent motor responses. In severe CTS, needle EMG of the APB is most helpful.

flashcards.front: What is the normal median motor distal latency?
flashcards.back: Less than 4.4ms (with a 6.5cm distance). F-wave less than 31ms. CV greater than 49 m/s. Amplitude greater than 4.2 mV.

flashcards.front: What is the Guyon's canal Type 4 lesion?
flashcards.back: Deep palmar motor branch only — weakness of the 1st-2nd lumbricals and ulnar-innervated thenar muscles. Hypothenar muscles are SPARED. Ulnar sensory is normal.

flashcards.front: Median motor: DL, CV, Amp?
flashcards.back: DL 4.5ms, CV 49 m/s, Amp 4.1 mV (recording from APB, 8cm distance). BOLDED = commonly performed.

flashcards.front: Ulnar motor: DL, CV, Amp?
flashcards.back: DL 3.7ms, CV 52/43 m/s (forearm/across elbow), Amp 6.0 mV (recording from ADM, 8cm). BOLDED = commonly performed.

flashcards.front: Peroneal motor: DL, CV, Amp?
flashcards.back: DL 6.5ms, CV 38/42 m/s, Amp 1.3 mV (recording from EDB, 8cm). Lowest amplitude of the commonly performed motor studies.

flashcards.front: Tibial motor: DL, CV, Amp?
flashcards.back: DL 6.1ms, CV 39 m/s, Amp 4.4 mV (recording from abd hallucis, 8cm). BOLDED = commonly performed.

flashcards.front: Median sensory antidromic: Lat and Amp?
flashcards.back: Palm (7cm): lat 2.4ms, amp 10 microvolts. Wrist (14cm): lat 4.0ms, amp 10 microvolts. BOLDED = commonly performed.

flashcards.front: Sural sensory: Lat and Amp?
flashcards.back: Lat 4.5ms, Amp 4 microvolts (recording at lateral ankle, stimulating posterior calf at 14cm). BOLDED = commonly performed.

flashcards.front: F-wave latencies: Median, Ulnar, Tibial, Peroneal?
flashcards.back: Median 31.4ms, Ulnar 31.1ms, Tibial 64.5ms, Peroneal 60.5ms. H-wave (tibial/soleus) 35.0ms. All BOLDED = commonly performed in clinical practice.

flashcards.front: Height correction: F-wave latencies for patients >180cm?
flashcards.back: Median 34.2ms, Ulnar 33.8ms, Tibial 70.4ms, Peroneal 63.6ms. Side-to-side differences: upper 2.2-2.5ms, lower 5.5-5.7ms.

flashcards.front: Sensory NCS machine settings?
flashcards.back: Gain: 20 microvolts/div. Filters: 10 (or 20) Hz to 2 kHz. Lower high-frequency filter than motor (2kHz vs 10kHz).

flashcards.front: Motor NCS machine settings?
flashcards.back: Gain: 5 mV/div. Filters: 10 Hz to 10 kHz. Higher gain and wider filter range than sensory NCS.

flashcards.front: EMG resting vs recruitment settings?
flashcards.back: Resting: 50 microvolts/div, 20 Hz to 10 kHz (sensitive for small spontaneous activity). Recruitment: 100-200 microvolts/div, 20 Hz to 10 kHz.

flashcards.front: Name the PRE-junctional EMG potentials.
flashcards.back: Fasciculation potentials (irregular, pop/thud), Myokymia (bursting, marching soldiers), Neuromyotonic discharges (Indy racing cars, Isaac's syndrome). All originate in the nerve.

flashcards.front: Name the POST-junctional EMG potentials.
flashcards.back: Fibrillation (regular, rain on tin roof), PSW (regular, dull thud), CRD (regular, machine/motorboat), Myotonia (wax/wane, dive bomber). All originate in the muscle fiber.

flashcards.front: What is a neuromyotonic discharge?
flashcards.back: Very high frequency discharge sounding like Indy racing cars, pre-junctional, tornado appearance. Associated with Isaac's syndrome (peripheral nerve hyperexcitability).

flashcards.front: Median nerve entrapment mnemonic?
flashcards.back: 'Lig PAC': Ligament of Struthers (rare), Pronator Teres Syndrome, AIN Syndrome (pure motor), CTS (carpal tunnel). Most common = CTS.

flashcards.front: Ulnar nerve entrapment mnemonic?
flashcards.back: 'ARC into Guyon's Canal': Arcade of Struthers, Retrocondylar/Ulnar Groove, Cubital Tunnel (most common), Guyon's Canal (dorsal ulnar cutaneous SPARED).

flashcards.front: CTS comparison technique thresholds?
flashcards.back: Median vs Ulnar digit 4 (14cm): 0.5ms or greater. Median vs Radial thumb (10cm): 0.5ms or greater. Palmar mixed median vs ulnar (8cm): 0.4ms or greater (most sensitive).

flashcards.front: Martin-Gruber anastomosis: prevalence and key findings?
flashcards.back: 15-20%. Median-to-ulnar motor crossover in forearm. False conduction block on ulnar (decreased proximal amp), increased proximal amp on median, initial positive dip on median recording hypothenar.

flashcards.front: Median nerve muscle mnemonic?
flashcards.back: '3 + AIN + LOAF': 3 forearm (PT, FCR, PL); AIN: FPL, FDP 1-2, PQ; LOAF: Lumbricals 1-2, Opponens, APB, FPB (superficial head).

flashcards.front: Ulnar nerve muscle mnemonic?
flashcards.back: 'IFA' or 'Forearm + LOAF + 3': FCU, FDP 3-4 (forearm); Interossei (all), FPB deep, ADM, ODM, FDM, Lumbricals 3-4, Adductor Pollicis.

flashcards.front: Radial nerve muscle mnemonic?
flashcards.back: 'TABES + PIN': Triceps, Anconeus, Brachioradialis, ECRL, Supinator (proximal); PIN: ECRB, EDC, ECU, APL, EPL, EPB, EIP (distal).

flashcards.front: MG vs LEMS vs Botulism: CMAP amplitude?
flashcards.back: MG = Normal CMAP. LEMS = Small CMAP. Botulism = Small CMAP. Small CMAP distinguishes pre-synaptic disorders (LEMS/Botulism) from post-synaptic (MG).

flashcards.front: MG vs LEMS vs Botulism: Fibs/PSWs?
flashcards.back: MG = No. LEMS = No. Botulism = YES. Botulism is the ONLY NMJ disorder with fibrillation potentials.

flashcards.front: SFEMG: what is MCD and what makes it abnormal?
flashcards.back: MCD = Mean Consecutive Difference between two time-locked potentials (measures jitter). Abnormal if >10% of pairs (2/20 or more) exceed the upper limit of normal for that muscle and age.

flashcards.front: NMJ evaluation order?
flashcards.back: 1) Routine NCS, 2) RNS (3Hz supramaximal), 3) Needle EMG, 4) SFEMG. Progress from least to most sensitive testing.

flashcards.front: SSR (Sympathetic Skin Response) basics?
flashcards.back: Latency 1000-1500ms (very slow — small fibers). Low frequency filter 0.5Hz. Stimulate with electrical, startle, or cough. Abnormal ONLY when absent. Sensitivity = low.

flashcards.front: Pre vs post-ganglionic neurotransmitters?
flashcards.back: Pre-ganglionic: ALL use acetylcholine (both parasympathetic and sympathetic). Post-ganglionic: Parasympathetic = ACh; Sympathetic (sweat glands) = ACh; Sympathetic (others) = Norepinephrine.

flashcards.front: ALS El Escorial criteria for 'definite' diagnosis?
flashcards.back: UMN + LMN signs in 3 of 4 regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral). 'Probable' = 2 regions with UMN rostral to LMN. EDX confirms LMN involvement.

flashcards.front: What is 'split hand syndrome' in ALS?
flashcards.back: Preferential wasting of thenar (APB) and first dorsal interosseous relative to hypothenar muscles. Relatively specific to ALS.

flashcards.front: Key ALS differential: MMNCB?
flashcards.back: Multifocal Motor Neuropathy with Conduction Block. Treatable with IVIg. Asymmetric distal weakness (upper limbs), motor conduction block on NCS, no sensory abnormalities, no UMN signs.

flashcards.front: EMG safety: pacemakers and central lines?
flashcards.back: Risk of current traveling along the needle or central line to the heart, potentially causing arrhythmia. Use extra caution with electrical stimulation near cardiac devices and central lines.

flashcards.front: EMG safety: pneumothorax risk?
flashcards.back: Risk when needling the serratus anterior, diaphragm, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, rhomboids, or paraspinal muscles at thoracic levels. Know the anatomy to avoid the pleural space.

flashcards.front: Forearm superficial flexor layer: muscles & nerves?
flashcards.back: Pronator teres (Median), FCR (Median), Palmaris longus (Median), FCU (Ulnar — the only ulnar-innervated superficial flexor), Brachioradialis (Radial). All median except FCU (ulnar) and brachioradialis (radial).

flashcards.front: FDP dual innervation?
flashcards.back: FDP to digits 2-3 = Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN, median branch). FDP to digits 4-5 = Ulnar nerve. Classic clinical distinction — explains why ulnar and median lesions produce different patterns of DIP flexion weakness.

flashcards.front: AIN (Anterior Interosseous Nerve): muscles & clinical test?
flashcards.back: Pure MOTOR branch of median. Innervates: FPL, FDP (digits 2-3), Pronator quadratus. Test: 'OK sign' — pinch thumb to index using tips (tests FPL + FDP-2). No sensory loss.

flashcards.front: EMG depth: Biceps vs Pronator teres vs Pronator quadratus?
flashcards.back: Biceps brachii: 3-6 Units/kg (deepest). Pronator teres: 1-2 Units/kg. Pronator quadratus: 0.5-1 Units/kg (shallowest). Brachioradialis & FDS: 1.5-3 Units/kg. FCR: 2-4 Units/kg.

flashcards.front: Wrist tendon landmarks radial to ulnar?
flashcards.back: FCR → Palmaris Longus → FCU. Median nerve runs between FCR and PL (or deep to PL). Palmaris longus absent in ~15% of population. Essential landmarks for NCS electrode placement.

flashcards.front: FCU: nerve, action, EMG significance?
flashcards.back: Ulnar nerve (C7-T1). Action: wrist flexion + ulnar deviation (adduction). EMG depth: 1.5-3 Units/kg. FIRST ulnar-innervated forearm muscle to test in cubital tunnel syndrome — abnormal FCU EMG localizes lesion to elbow or above.

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus mnemonic: levels?
flashcards.back: 'Risk Takers Don't Cautiously Behave' = Roots (C5-T1) → Trunks (superior, middle, inferior) → Divisions (anterior, posterior) → Cords (lateral, posterior, medial) → Branches (terminal nerves).

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus: 3 trunks?
flashcards.back: Superior trunk: C5 + C6 (gives suprascapular nerve). Middle trunk: C7 alone. Inferior trunk: C8 + T1. Erb-Duchenne palsy = upper trunk (C5-C6). Klumpke palsy = lower trunk (C8-T1).

flashcards.front: Brachial plexus: 3 cords & naming?
flashcards.back: Lateral cord (anterior divisions of superior + middle trunk). Posterior cord (all 3 posterior divisions). Medial cord (anterior division of inferior trunk). Named by position relative to the AXILLARY ARTERY.

flashcards.front: Median nerve: cord origin?
flashcards.back: Unique dual origin — lateral head from LATERAL cord + medial head from MEDIAL cord. They join anterior to the axillary artery. This is why it's called 'median' — forms in the middle from both sides.

flashcards.front: Posterior cord terminal branches?
flashcards.back: Axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor, regimental badge area sensation) and Radial nerve (triceps, all extensors of wrist/fingers, dorsal hand sensation). Both arise from the posterior cord.

flashcards.front: Erb-Duchenne palsy vs Klumpke palsy?
flashcards.back: Erb-Duchenne: Upper trunk C5-C6 injury. 'Waiter's tip' — arm internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated. Klumpke: Lower trunk C8-T1 injury. Hand intrinsic weakness + claw hand ± Horner syndrome (T1 sympathetic involvement).

flashcards.front: Median nerve at elbow: classic sign?
flashcards.back: 'Hand of Benediction' — when trying to make a fist, digits 1 & 2 remain extended (FDS & FDP to those digits paralyzed). All forearm median muscles affected (PT, FCR, PL, FDS, AIN muscles) plus thenar & lumbricals 1-2.

flashcards.front: Median nerve at wrist (CTS): classic sign?
flashcards.back: 'Ape Hand' — thenar eminence wasting with loss of thumb opposition (APB, opponens pollicis affected). Forearm muscles SPARED (innervated above the wrist). Diagnosis: Phalen maneuver (wrist flexion 60s) + Tinel sign (percussion over carpal tunnel).

flashcards.front: Radial nerve at spiral groove: classic sign?
flashcards.back: 'Wrist Drop' — cannot extend wrist or fingers. Triceps SPARED (innervated proximal to spiral groove). Sensory loss: dorsal hand/1st web space. Common cause: 'Saturday night palsy' (arm over chair), humeral shaft fracture.

flashcards.front: PIN syndrome vs radial nerve at spiral groove?
flashcards.back: PIN = pure motor. Causes 'finger drop' WITHOUT wrist drop (ECRL spared → wrist can extend but deviates radially). NO sensory loss. Spiral groove = wrist drop + finger drop + sensory loss dorsal hand. Triceps spared in both.

flashcards.front: Ulnar paradox: explain?
flashcards.back: Claw hand is WORSE with DISTAL (wrist/Guyon canal) ulnar lesion. Why? With proximal lesion, FDP 4-5 is also paralyzed so fingers can't flex at DIP → less clawing. With distal lesion, FDP works (innervated above) → unopposed DIP/PIP flexion → more dramatic claw.

flashcards.front: Axillary nerve injury: motor, sensory, cause?
flashcards.back: Motor: deltoid (can't abduct past 15°) + teres minor. Sensory: 'regimental badge area' (lateral shoulder patch). Common cause: anterior shoulder dislocation. The nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus through the quadrilateral space.

flashcards.front: Long thoracic nerve injury: sign & causes?
flashcards.back: 'Winged scapula' — medial border of scapula protrudes posteriorly, worse when pushing against wall. Serratus anterior paralyzed. Causes: surgery (axillary dissection), heavy backpack, viral neuritis (Parsonage-Turner). Nerve = C5-C7 roots.

flashcards.front: Anterior upper extremity cutaneous innervation: proximal to distal?
flashcards.back: Axillary n. (upper lateral cutaneous n. of arm — shoulder) → Radial n. (lower lateral cutaneous n. of arm) → Musculocutaneous n. (lateral cutaneous n. of forearm) → Median n. (palmar hand, lateral 3½ digits). Medial side: medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm.

flashcards.front: Posterior upper extremity cutaneous innervation?
flashcards.back: Radial nerve DOMINATES: posterior cutaneous n. of arm (post arm) → posterior cutaneous n. of forearm (post forearm) → superficial branch (dorsal hand/1st web space). Also: supraclavicular nn. (shoulder cap), intercostobrachial (medial arm), ulnar (medial 1½ digits dorsally).

flashcards.front: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve: clinical pearl?
flashcards.back: Runs adjacent to the BASILIC VEIN in the medial arm/forearm. Vulnerable during venipuncture, IV access, and PICC line placement at the antecubital fossa. Injury causes numbness/paresthesias along the medial forearm. Arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus.

flashcards.front: Lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm: which nerve?
flashcards.back: Terminal sensory branch of the MUSCULOCUTANEOUS nerve. After innervating biceps, brachialis, and coracobrachialis, it emerges lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The LABC sensory NCS tests the musculocutaneous nerve.

flashcards.front: Superficial branch of radial nerve: territory?
flashcards.back: Sensory to the dorsum of the hand and dorsal aspects of the lateral 3½ digits (proximal phalanges). Pure sensory — emerges from under brachioradialis in the distal forearm. Tested clinically by the superficial radial sensory NCS (antidromic, recording at anatomic snuffbox).

flashcards.front: Forearm deep flexor compartment muscles?
flashcards.back: FDP (flexor digitorum profundus — dual innervation: AIN for digits 2-3, ulnar for 4-5), FPL (flexor pollicis longus — AIN), Pronator quadratus (AIN). ALL deep flexors are AIN or ulnar innervated. FPL is absent in the images — unique thumb muscle.

flashcards.front: Forearm intermediate flexor layer?
flashcards.back: Contains only ONE muscle: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis (FDS). Median nerve (C7-T1). Action: PIP flexion of digits 2-5 (DIP remains free). EMG depth: 1.5-3 Units/kg. Tested by holding other fingers extended while flexing one PIP joint.

flashcards.front: Suprascapular nerve: origin & muscles?
flashcards.back: Arises from the SUPERIOR TRUNK (C5-C6), NOT from a cord. Innervates supraspinatus (first 15° of abduction) and infraspinatus (external rotation). Injury = difficulty initiating abduction + weak external rotation. Can be compressed at suprascapular notch.

flashcards.front: Upper limb nerves: anterior view course?
flashcards.back: From lateral to medial at elbow: Radial nerve (deep, wraps posteriorly), Musculocutaneous (lateral, between biceps/brachialis), Median (middle, crosses elbow at cubital fossa), Ulnar (medial, behind medial epicondyle). All travel distally into forearm/hand with their respective muscle groups.

flashcards.front: Median motor: E1 placement on APB?
flashcards.back: Most prominent part of thenar eminence, midway between midpoint of wrist crease and 1st MCP joint. E2 on proximal phalanx of thumb. Ground on dorsum of hand. Wrist stim 8cm proximal between FCR and PL tendons.

flashcards.front: Median motor: normal values (DL, Amp, CV)?
flashcards.back: DL ≤ 4.5 ms | Amp ≥ 4.1 mV | CV ≥ 49 m/s. Distance: 8 cm wrist-to-E1. Machine: 2Hz-10kHz filters, 2ms/div sweep, 1mV/div sensitivity.

flashcards.front: Ulnar motor: E1 placement on ADM?
flashcards.back: Midpoint of 5th metacarpal bone over ADM belly. E2 on 5th MCP joint. Wrist stim 8cm proximal, medial wrist lateral to FCU tendon. BE: 3-4cm distal to medial epicondyle. AE: 10cm proximal to BE. ELBOW FLEXED 70-90°.

flashcards.front: Ulnar motor: normal values & across-elbow criteria?
flashcards.back: DL ≤ 3.7 ms | Amp ≥ 6.0 mV | CV ≥ 52 m/s (forearm) | CV ≥ 43 m/s (across elbow). AE-BE distance must be ≥10 cm measured with elbow flexed. CV across elbow normally up to 10 m/s slower than forearm.

flashcards.front: Peroneal motor: E1 placement on EDB?
flashcards.back: Dorsolateral foot over EDB belly — visible prominence in line with inferior border of lateral malleolus. E2 on 5th MTP joint. THREE stim sites required: ankle (8cm), below fibular head (BFH), and popliteal fossa (10-12cm above BFH).

flashcards.front: Peroneal motor: normal values & key facts?
flashcards.back: DL ≤ 6.5 ms | Amp ≥ 1.3 mV (LOWEST of all 4!) | CV ≥ 41 m/s. BFH requires higher stim current (nerve is deep). EDB can atrophy — may need tibialis anterior. Popliteal fossa excess stim → co-stimulates tibial nerve.

flashcards.front: Tibial motor: E1 placement on AH?
flashcards.back: 1 cm proximal and 1 cm inferior to navicular prominence, midway between 1st MTP and heel along medial arch. E2 on 1st MTP joint. Ankle stim: posterior to medial malleolus, 8cm from E1. Popliteal: mid-fossa over popliteal pulse.

flashcards.front: Tibial motor: normal values & critical pitfall?
flashcards.back: DL ≤ 6.1 ms | Amp ≥ 4.4 mV | CV ≥ 41 m/s. CRITICAL: Normal 21-50% amplitude drop between ankle and popliteal fossa — do NOT call this conduction block! It's normal phase cancellation over the long nerve segment.

flashcards.front: Median sensory: technique (antidromic)?
flashcards.back: Ring electrodes on digit 2 or 3 (digit 3 preferred). E1 on proximal phalanx, E2 3-4cm distal. Stim at wrist 14cm proximal between FCR and PL. Normal: onset ≤ 2.4 ms (or peak ≤ 3.6 ms), Amp ≥ 10 µV. Filters: 20Hz-2kHz, 10-20 µV/div.

flashcards.front: Ulnar sensory: technique (antidromic)?
flashcards.back: Ring electrodes on digit 5. E1 on proximal phalanx, E2 3-4cm distal. Stim at wrist 14cm proximal, medial wrist lateral to FCU. Normal: latency ≤ 4.0 ms, Amp ≥ 6 µV. CTS comparison to digit 4: median-ulnar diff ≥ 0.5ms = abnormal.

flashcards.front: Sural sensory: technique?
flashcards.back: E1 posterior to lateral malleolus. E2 3-4cm distal. Stim posterolateral calf 14cm proximal. Normal: peak latency ≤ 4.5 ms, Amp ≥ 4 µV. Patient prone or lateral with leg up. Shorter distances (10-12cm) give better responses. NORMAL in radiculopathy.

flashcards.front: Initial positive deflection: meaning & fix?
flashcards.back: On ANY motor NCS, initial positive (downward) deflection = E1 is NOT over the motor point. The CMAP is approaching E1 from a distance. FIX: reposition E1 toward muscle belly until clean negative (upward) initial deflection appears.

flashcards.front: Standard distances: motor vs sensory?
flashcards.back: ALL motor studies: 8 cm (wrist/ankle to E1). ALL sensory studies: 14 cm (wrist to digit / calf to malleolus). Palmar mixed nerve: 7 cm (midpalm across carpal tunnel). These are FIXED — changing distance changes latency!

flashcards.front: Temperature requirements for NCS?
flashcards.back: Hand: ≥ 32°C. Leg: ≥ 30°C. Cold PROLONGS latencies, SLOWS CV, and counterintuitively INCREASES amplitudes (cold slows Na+ channel inactivation → prolonged action potentials). Always warm limb if below threshold before testing.

flashcards.front: Supramaximal stimulation: definition?
flashcards.back: Increase stimulus intensity 20-25% ABOVE the level producing maximal CMAP/SNAP amplitude. Ensures ALL nerve fibers are activated. Typical: 15-20 mA at wrist, higher at deeper sites (popliteal fossa, BFH). Never >50 mA in children.

flashcards.front: Accessory peroneal nerve: what is it & how to confirm?
flashcards.back: Branch from superficial peroneal that courses BEHIND the lateral malleolus to innervate lateral EDB. Suspect when ankle CMAP < BFH CMAP. Confirm: stimulate behind lateral malleolus → get a CMAP. This CMAP + ankle CMAP ≈ proximal CMAP.

flashcards.front: Martin-Gruber anastomosis: effects on NCS?
flashcards.back: Median-to-ulnar crossover in forearm (15-20%). Effects: (1) Median motor CMAP may be larger at elbow than wrist, (2) Ulnar motor CMAP larger at AE than BE, (3) Can mimic conduction block. The crossover fibers are usually to FDI, not ADM — so recording from FDI makes it more apparent.

flashcards.front: Cubital tunnel: key NCS findings?
flashcards.back: CV across elbow < 43 m/s OR >10 m/s drop from forearm CV. Amplitude drop AE-to-BE >20% with <15% temporal dispersion = conduction block. DUC sensory: may be abnormal (branches proximal to wrist). Inching study: 1-2cm increments across elbow to localize precisely.

flashcards.front: Sensory NCS: radiculopathy vs plexopathy?
flashcards.back: In RADICULOPATHY, sensory NCS are NORMAL (lesion is pre-ganglionic — DRG and peripheral axons intact). In PLEXOPATHY, sensory NCS are ABNORMAL (lesion is post-ganglionic). This distinction is one of the most important principles in electrodiagnostic medicine.

flashcards.front: Ground electrode placement rule?
flashcards.back: ALWAYS between the stimulating and recording electrodes. Reduces stimulus artifact and electrical noise. Essential for clean recordings, especially small sensory potentials. Can be surface pad or strap electrode on dorsum of hand/foot.
