clinical.title: Clinical Approach to the EDX Study FOUNDATION
clinical.lead: The electrodiagnostic (EDX) study is an extension of the neurologic examination — not a fixed recipe. Every study is planned from a focused history and exam, then refined in real time as results arrive. This section walks through the patient encounter, lesion localization, building a differential, and turning it into a concrete list of nerves and muscles to test.
clinical.html:
1 · The Patient Encounter — Why It Comes First

EDX testing confirms, localizes, and characterizes a lesion that is already suspected on clinical grounds. Before a single electrode goes on, you should have a working hypothesis built from a brief, directed history and examination. A panel run without a hypothesis misses lesions, over-tests, and wastes the patient's limited tolerance for discomfort.

Five questions a well-planned study answers:

  • Where is the lesion? (localization)
  • What is the underlying process? (axonal vs demyelinating, focal vs diffuse)
  • How severe is it? (degree of axon loss / conduction failure)
  • How old is it? (acute vs chronic — timing of denervation and reinnervation)
  • Is it still active? (ongoing denervation vs stable/old injury)
Principle: the plan is dynamic. Each result changes the next step — an unexpected finding should redirect the study, not be ignored to finish a pre-set list.

2 · Focused History

Characterize the complaint

  • Symptom type: weakness, numbness/tingling, pain, cramps, fasciculations, or fatigue?
  • Time course: acute, subacute, or chronic? Progressive, static, or relapsing? Worse with sustained activity (fatigable)?
  • Distribution: focal vs generalized, symmetric vs asymmetric, proximal vs distal, length-dependent?
  • Provoking factors: position, repetitive activity, time of day.

Relevant background

  • Past medical history: diabetes, thyroid or renal disease, chemotherapy, alcohol use, HIV, prior trauma, surgery, or radiation.
  • Medications & toxins with neuropathic potential.
  • Family history: pes cavus, hammertoes, or a "clumsy" gait since childhood point toward an inherited neuropathy.

3 · Focused Physical Examination

A few targeted findings sharpen the differential and tell you where to concentrate the study.

Exam elementNormalWhat an abnormal finding suggests
InspectionNo wastingAtrophy (chronic lower-motor-neuron loss); fasciculations (motor neuron/anterior horn cell); deformity or scars
ToneNormalDecreased → lower motor neuron; increased/spastic → upper motor neuron
Strength (MRC 0–5)5/5Pattern matters: proximal → myopathy or NMJ; distal → neuropathy; focal → single nerve or root
Reflexes2+Reduced/absent → radiculopathy, neuropathy, LMN; brisk → upper motor neuron
SensationIntactDermatomal → root; single-nerve territory → mononeuropathy; stocking-glove → polyneuropathy. Note modality: large-fiber (vibration, proprioception) vs small-fiber (pain, temperature)
Provocative maneuvers: Tinel & Phalen (median at the wrist), elbow-flexion test (ulnar at the elbow), Spurling (cervical root), straight-leg raise (lumbosacral root).

4 · Localization — Where Is the Lesion?

EDX reasoning walks the motor and sensory unit from the spinal cord outward. Each level carries a characteristic clinical and electrodiagnostic signature.

LevelClinical cluesEDX signature
Anterior horn cellPainless weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, no sensory lossNormal SNAPs; reduced CMAP; widespread neurogenic changes (incl. bulbar/thoracic); no conduction block
Root (radiculopathy)Dermatomal sensory symptoms, myotomal weakness, reduced reflexNormal SNAPs (lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion); needle changes in the myotome incl. paraspinals
PlexusSymptoms crossing more than one nerve and root in a single limbAbnormal SNAPs; needle changes cross nerve & root boundaries; paraspinals spared
Peripheral nerveSingle nerve (mono-), asymmetric/patchy (multiplex), or distal-symmetric (poly-)Focal slowing or block at entrapment sites; low SNAP/CMAP; length-dependent pattern in polyneuropathy
Neuromuscular junctionFatigable weakness; ocular/bulbar (MG) or proximal + autonomic (LEMS)Routine NCS normal; decrement on slow repetitive stimulation (MG); increment after exercise (LEMS)
MuscleSymmetric proximal weakness, no sensory loss, reflexes preserved earlyNormal NCS; small, brief, polyphasic MUAPs with early recruitment; ± fibrillations
The single most useful discriminator: the sensory nerve action potential (SNAP). A preserved SNAP in a numb area points proximal to the dorsal root ganglion (radiculopathy); a reduced SNAP places the lesion at or distal to the ganglion (plexus or peripheral nerve).

5 · From Pattern to Differential — Worked Examples

The symptom pattern narrows the differential, and the differential dictates the study. Common bread-and-butter presentations:

PresentationDifferential to resolveWhere EDX focuses
Numbness/tingling of the ring & little fingersUlnar neuropathy (elbow > wrist), lower-trunk/medial-cord plexopathy, C8–T1 radiculopathyUlnar motor with across-elbow segment (± inching); ulnar & dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory; needle FDI, ADM, FCU, C8–T1 paraspinals
Numbness of the thumb, index & middle fingersMedian neuropathy at the wrist (CTS), C6–C7 radiculopathy, upper trunkMedian vs ulnar sensory/palmar comparison studies; median motor; needle APB, pronator teres, cervical paraspinals
Slowly progressive proximal weaknessMyopathy, NMJ disorder, motor neuron disease, or a proximal neuropathy (e.g., CIDP)NCS to screen nerve integrity; repetitive stimulation for NMJ; needle proximal + distal muscles for MUAP morphology & recruitment
Foot dropPeroneal neuropathy at the fibular head, L5 radiculopathy, sciatic or lumbosacral plexus lesionPeroneal motor across the fibular head (block?); superficial peroneal sensory (spared in L5 root); needle TA, EDB, tibialis posterior, short head of biceps femoris, L5 paraspinals
Distal symmetric numbness (stocking-glove)Length-dependent polyneuropathy (diabetic and others)Bilateral sural & peroneal/tibial; add upper-limb sensory; needle distal > proximal to grade the length-dependence

6 · Building the EDX Plan

Nerve conduction studies

  • Choose the motor & sensory nerves that test your hypothesis.
  • Compare side-to-side and to the asymptomatic limb.
  • Add across-joint segments where entrapment is suspected (e.g., across the elbow, across the fibular head).

Needle EMG

  • Sample muscles that share a nerve but different roots (and vice versa) to separate root vs nerve vs plexus.
  • Include paraspinals when a radiculopathy is on the list.
  • Assess both MUAP morphology and recruitment.

Special studies, added by hypothesis:

  • Repetitive nerve stimulation — suspected NMJ disorder (decrement in MG; increment/facilitation in LEMS).
  • F-waves — proximal segments, early Guillain-Barré, polyneuropathy.
  • H-reflex — S1 radiculopathy and the proximal tibial pathway.
  • Blink reflex — facial nerve, trigeminal, or brainstem pathways.
The plan is a starting point, not a script. Confirm, extend, or drop branches as data arrives — an unexpected conduction block, for example, should send you looking for demyelination in other nerves.

7 · Etiology & Characterization

Once the lesion is localized, EDX helps characterize the process — findings that steer the differential and the downstream workup.

  • Acquired vs inherited: family history, foot deformity, and very uniform slowing favor an inherited process.
  • Axonal vs demyelinating: low amplitudes point to axon loss; marked slowing, conduction block, and temporal dispersion point to demyelination.
  • Acute vs chronic: fibrillation potentials appear roughly 2–3 weeks after axon loss; large, long-duration reinnervating MUAPs indicate a chronic process.
  • Active vs inactive: ongoing fibrillations signal active denervation; their absence with stable large MUAPs suggests an old, inactive injury.
This clinical-approach section is an original educational summary of standard electrodiagnostic practice (patient encounter, localization, and study planning). Always follow your own laboratory's protocols and your supervising physician's direction.

procedures.title: ★ Common Procedures High Yield
procedures.lead: The 22 areas below are the core knowledge base for hands-on NCS/EMG practice. Focus on these to rebuild your clinical foundation — every practice question and flashcard maps back to one of these procedure cards.
procedures.html:
1

Waveform Identification

Spontaneous & abnormal potentials
  • Fibrillation potentials: duration <5ms, amplitude <1mV, fire with a regular rhythm, initial POSITIVE deflection (biphasic/triphasic), single denervated muscle fiber, sound = "rain on a tin roof."
  • Positive sharp waves (PSWs): same generator as fibrillations; sharp initial positive deflection with a long slow negative return ("sawtooth"); regular firing; sound = dull thud.
  • CRDs (complex repetitive discharges): abrupt onset and offset, no wax/wane, uniform repeating waveform via ephaptic transmission between adjacent fibers; sound = machine gun.
  • Fasciculation potentials: irregular firing, 1 Hz up to many/minute, whole motor unit morphology; can be benign or pathologic (ALS, radiculopathy).
  • Myotonic discharges: wax AND wane in both amplitude and frequency; sound = "dive bomber" / motorcycle revving.
  • End-plate spikes (MEPP-related): duration 0.5–2ms, amplitude 10–50µV, initial NEGATIVE deflection, irregular, occur only in the end-plate zone, often painful to the patient.
  • End-plate noise: low-amplitude (10–40µV), monophasic negative "seashell roar," represents subthreshold MEPPs.
  • Myokymia: grouped/repetitive discharges of the same motor unit firing in bursts at regular intervals ("marching soldiers").
  • Cramp potentials: high-frequency (up to 150Hz), involuntary, painful motor unit discharges.
Pearl: Fibrillations = initial positive; end-plate spikes = initial negative. This single feature is the most critical discriminator you'll use in clinical practice.
2

Nerve Conduction Studies Interpretation

CMAP / SNAP fundamentals
  • CMAP is recorded with a belly-tendon montage (active over the motor point, reference over the tendon); amplitude reflects the number of functioning motor axons/muscle fibers.
  • SNAP: only large, fast-conducting myelinated sensory axons contribute — slower fibers desynchronize and cancel out of the summated potential.
  • Conduction velocity = distance ÷ time, using the latency difference between two stimulation sites (not the distal latency alone).
  • Side-to-side CMAP amplitude difference >50% is considered abnormal (supports axon loss).
  • Temporal dispersion: normal distal CMAPs are more synchronized (taller/shorter duration) than proximal CMAPs; excessive dispersion suggests demyelination.
  • Normal values are lab- and temperature-dependent — always confirm local reference ranges.
Pearl: CV = distance/time — e.g., 260mm over a 4ms latency difference = 65 m/s. You'll perform this calculation routinely when interpreting your NCS results.
3

Temperature Effects

The single most-missed technical factor
  • Cooling the limb → increases amplitude, increases duration, decreases conduction velocity, and increases distal latency.
  • CV decreases by roughly 2.4 m/s per °C below 32°C in the upper limb.
  • Distal latency increases by roughly 0.2 ms per °C of cooling.
  • Recommended surface temperatures: 32°C for the upper limb, 30°C for the lower limb (measured with a skin thermometer).
  • A cold limb can mimic demyelinating slowing and false-positive "focal" latency prolongation — always warm the limb rather than just applying a correction factor.
Pearl: Cold slows nerves down but makes waveforms bigger and wider — this apparent paradox (slower CV yet larger amplitude) is a common pitfall that can lead to misinterpretation if you don't warm the limb first.
4

Needle EMG Examination

Insertional, spontaneous, and voluntary activity
  • Insertional activity: normal burst lasts <300ms with a concentric needle and <230ms with a monopolar needle after needle movement stops.
  • Spontaneous activity assessed at rest: fibrillations, PSWs, CRDs, myotonic discharges, fasciculations, myokymia.
  • MUAP analysis: duration (baseline departure to return — reflects number of fibers in the motor unit), amplitude (reflects fibers nearest the electrode), phases (normal ≤4), and recruitment.
  • Interference pattern: normal = full pattern at maximal effort (individual MUAPs indistinguishable); reduced = neurogenic; early/full at low effort with small units = myopathic.
  • Normal recruitment firing rate is 5–10 Hz before the next motor unit is recruited.
Pearl: A patient with give-way/psychogenic weakness shows a normal, full recruitment pattern despite reduced effort clinically — needle EMG "sees through" non-organic weakness.
5

Clinical Localization

Radiculopathy vs plexopathy vs neuropathy vs NMJ vs myopathy
  • Radiculopathy (preganglionic): SNAPs are normal even with sensory symptoms (DRG and distal sensory axon intact); paraspinal denervation is the key localizing finding.
  • Plexopathy (postganglionic): SNAPs are abnormal; paraspinals are spared (normal).
  • Peripheral (mono)neuropathy: findings confined to a single nerve's distribution, often with focal slowing/conduction block at an entrapment site.
  • NMJ disorder: normal SNAPs, normal (or low in LEMS) resting CMAP, abnormal repetitive stimulation, normal-to-mildly-unstable MUAPs, no fibrillations typically.
  • Myopathy: normal SNAPs/CVs, short-duration low-amplitude polyphasic MUAPs with early recruitment; fibrillations possible in inflammatory myopathy.
Pearl: Paraspinal involvement = radiculopathy. Normal SNAPs despite sensory complaints = preganglionic (root) lesion. These two facts resolve most localization questions.
6

Entrapment Neuropathies

The classic compression sites
  • CTS: median nerve at the wrist; the wrist-to-palm segment is the most sensitive for early disease, but also the most vulnerable to measurement error because the distance is short.
  • Ulnar neuropathy: elbow (cubital tunnel, most common site) vs Guyon's canal (wrist) — dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensation is spared in Guyon's canal lesions since that branch arises proximal to the wrist.
  • Fibular neuropathy at the fibular head — the most common lower-limb entrapment; short head of biceps femoris is spared (innervated proximal to the fibular head).
  • Tarsal tunnel syndrome: tibial nerve entrapment behind the medial malleolus.
  • Thoracic outlet syndrome (true neurogenic): affects the lower trunk (C8-T1); medial antebrachial cutaneous and ulnar SNAPs abnormal, median SNAP normal.
  • Suprascapular nerve entrapment: notch lesion affects supraspinatus + infraspinatus; spinoglenoid notch lesion affects infraspinatus only.
Pearl: Froment's sign (compensatory thumb IP flexion via median-innervated FPL) indicates ulnar nerve palsy with adductor pollicis weakness. "Handlebar palsy" = ulnar neuropathy at the wrist.
7

Brachial Plexus Anatomy

Roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches
  • Roots C5-T1 → Trunks: upper (C5-6), middle (C7), lower (C8-T1) → anterior/posterior Divisions → Cords named for their relation to the axillary artery.
  • Posterior cord → axillary + radial nerves (terminal), plus upper/lower subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves.
  • Lateral cord → musculocutaneous nerve + lateral contribution to the median nerve.
  • Medial cord → ulnar nerve + medial contribution to the median nerve.
  • Root-level branches: dorsal scapular nerve (C5, rhomboids), long thoracic nerve (C5-7, serratus anterior).
  • Erb's palsy = upper trunk (C5-6) — deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps ("waiter's tip"). Klumpke's palsy = lower trunk (C8-T1) — hand intrinsics ± Horner's syndrome.
Pearl: Median sensory fibers travel via the upper + middle trunks (lateral cord); median motor fibers to the hand travel via the lower trunk (medial cord contribution).
8

Lumbosacral Anatomy

Lumbar & sacral plexus essentials
  • Femoral nerve: L2-4, posterior divisions; runs lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle (vulnerable there).
  • Obturator nerve: L2-4, anterior rami; exits through the obturator foramen; innervates the hip adductors.
  • Sciatic nerve: L4-S3, formed from medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) trunks; the fibular division is more vulnerable to injury than the tibial division.
  • Localization tools: adductor longus (obturator, L2-4) helps confirm an L3-4 root lesion vs a femoral neuropathy; short head of biceps femoris (fibular division of sciatic, innervated above the fibular head) helps distinguish a sciatic lesion from an isolated fibular neuropathy at the knee.
  • Gluteal nerves: superior gluteal (L4-S1) → gluteus medius/minimus, TFL; inferior gluteal (L5-S2) → gluteus maximus.
Pearl: An abnormal short head of biceps femoris in a "foot drop" points to the sciatic nerve or more proximal — not an isolated fibular neuropathy.
9

Anomalous Innervation

Don't mistake anatomy for pathology
  • Martin-Gruber anastomosis: median (or AIN)-to-ulnar motor fiber crossover in the forearm, present in roughly 15–30% of people. Classic clue: stimulating the median nerve proximally while recording over ulnar-innervated hypothenar muscle produces a volume-conducted initial positive deflection, and can create a pseudo-conduction-block pattern on ulnar studies.
  • Accessory deep peroneal nerve: present in up to 28% of people; supplies the lateral portion of extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) via a branch that courses posterior to the lateral malleolus.
  • Confirm an accessory deep peroneal nerve by stimulating just posterior/inferior to the lateral malleolus while still recording from EDB — this "makes up" the amplitude difference between distal (ankle) and proximal (knee) stimulation.
Pearl: Anomalous CMAP with an unexpectedly LARGER proximal-than-distal peroneal response should raise suspicion for an accessory deep peroneal nerve before you call it pathologic conduction block.
10

Nerve Injury Classification

Seddon & Sunderland, and the Wallerian timeline
  • Seddon: Neurapraxia (focal conduction block, axon intact, best prognosis) → Axonotmesis (axon disrupted, Wallerian degeneration, connective tissue framework preserved, regeneration ~1mm/day) → Neurotmesis (complete disruption, no spontaneous recovery).
  • Sunderland 1st–5th degree parallels Seddon, subdividing axonotmesis by which connective tissue layers (endoneurium, perineurium) remain intact.
  • Wallerian degeneration timeline: motor NCS becomes abnormal distally by day 3-5; sensory NCS by day 6-10.
  • Fibrillations appear at 10-14 days in proximal muscles and 3-4 weeks in distal muscles post-injury.
  • Immediately after axonotmesis (before fibrillations appear), the earliest EMG change is reduced recruitment.
Pearl: Early after an acute injury, distal stimulation can still look falsely normal until Wallerian degeneration completes — timing your study matters as much as the findings themselves.
11

NMJ Disorders

MG vs LEMS vs botulism
  • Myasthenia Gravis: postsynaptic, AChR antibodies, >10% decrement at 2-3Hz RNS, normal resting CMAP amplitude, thymoma association.
  • LEMS: presynaptic, VGCC antibodies, low resting CMAP amplitude, >100% increment with brief exercise or rapid RNS, strongly associated with small cell lung cancer.
  • Botulism: presynaptic (SNARE cleavage), low CMAPs with an incremental response pattern similar to LEMS; infantile botulism presents with constipation, hypotonia, and bulbar symptoms.
  • Safety factor = ACh released ÷ ACh needed to reach threshold; a reduced safety factor is the shared final mechanism across all NMJ disorders.
Pearl: Low RNS (2-3Hz) unmasks MG (decrement); high-rate RNS or post-exercise testing unmasks LEMS/botulism (increment). Knowing which direction to test is essential when you encounter a patient with suspected NMJ disorder.
12

Late Responses

F-wave, H-reflex, A-wave, blink reflex
  • F-wave: antidromic motor neuron activation, supramaximal stimulus, variable latency/morphology trial-to-trial, amplitude ~1-5% of the CMAP.
  • H-reflex: true monosynaptic reflex arc, submaximal stimulus, stable latency and amplitude; classic sites are tibial/soleus (S1) and median/FCR (C6-7).
  • A-wave (axon reflex): constant latency and morphology, appears between the M-wave and F-wave, best elicited at moderate stimulus intensities.
  • Blink reflex: R1 = early, ipsilateral only (trigeminal → pons → facial); R2 = later, bilateral (trigeminal → medulla → bilateral facial).
Pearl: "Variable = F-wave, stable = H-reflex" is the fastest way to separate these two on a tracing-based question.
13

Recruitment & Motor Unit Analysis

Neurogenic vs myopathic patterns
  • Normal firing rate at recruitment threshold is 5-10 Hz; normal recruitment ratio (firing rate ÷ number of units recruited) is ≤5.
  • Neurogenic: reduced recruitment (fewer available units) + increased firing rate of the remaining units; chronically, large-amplitude/long-duration MUAPs.
  • Myopathic: early/full recruitment with small, short-duration, polyphasic MUAPs (more units needed for a given force).
  • Duration reflects the number of muscle fibers in the motor unit; amplitude reflects fiber density immediately adjacent to the electrode.
  • Turns-amplitude analysis (Stålberg method): quantitative interference-pattern technique useful when individual MUAP analysis or patient cooperation is limited.
Pearl: Chronic poliomyelitis is the classic "pure chronic neurogenic" pattern — large, long-duration MUAPs with reduced recruitment but few/no fibrillations (fully remodeled).
14

Polyneuropathy Patterns

Axonal vs demyelinating, acquired vs hereditary
  • Axonal: decreased CMAP/SNAP amplitudes with relatively preserved conduction velocities.
  • Demyelinating: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities, conduction block, and temporal dispersion.
  • AIDP (Guillain-Barré): earliest electrodiagnostic finding is absent or prolonged F-waves (and/or absent H-reflexes); conduction block and dispersion develop later.
  • Anti-MAG neuropathy: disproportionately severe distal motor latency prolongation with IgM paraproteinemia.
  • Hereditary (CMT1/HNPP): uniform slowing across nerves with no conduction block, unlike patchy acquired demyelination (CIDP).
Pearl: Uniform slowing = hereditary; patchy slowing with conduction block/dispersion = acquired. This single rule is the key to differentiating CMT1 from CIDP when you see demyelinating features on your studies.
15

MUAP Analysis (Motor Unit Action Potentials)

Duration, amplitude, phases, recruitment, and pathology patterns
  • Duration: reflects the total number of muscle fibers in the motor unit; normal range roughly 5-15ms — the single most important MUAP parameter.
  • Amplitude: normal 100µV-2mV; a high-frequency component reflecting only the 2-12 fibers nearest the needle — "correlates with volume, not pitch."
  • Phases: normally 2-4; >10% polyphasia is abnormal in most muscles — the deltoid is the exception, where up to 25% polyphasic is normal.
  • Rise time: should be <500µs; a longer rise time means the needle is not close enough to the motor unit being analyzed.
  • Stability: unstable MUAPs point to NMJ disorders, early reinnervation, or myopathic conditions.
  • Satellite potentials: small potentials time-locked to (trailing) the main MUAP from slow conduction in immature collateral sprouts during early reinnervation; the immature NMJ fires intermittently, making the satellite unstable.
  • Recruitment ratio (firing rate ÷ number of MUAPs) is normally about 5:1; initial firing pattern is semi-rhythmic at 4-5 Hz.
  • Activation (central — firing rate) vs Recruitment (peripheral — adding motor units): CNS lesions reduce activation; peripheral lesions reduce recruitment.
  • Size principle: small Type I (slow-twitch) motor neurons fire first; large Type II (fast-twitch) motor neurons are recruited only with maximal contraction.
  • Table 15-2 patterns: Acute neuropathic-axonal = normal MUAPs + decreased recruitment; Chronic neuropathic = large/long/polyphasic MUAPs + decreased recruitment; Myopathic = short/small/polyphasic + early/normal recruitment; Nascent (early reinnervation) = short/small/polyphasic with reduced recruitment; CNS = normal MUAPs with reduced activation (not recruitment).
Pearl: Nascent motor units vs myopathic MUAPs — both are short, small, and polyphasic, but nascent units have REDUCED recruitment while myopathic units have EARLY/normal recruitment.
16

Ulnar Nerve — Detailed NCS Protocol

Motor/sensory technique, elbow positioning, and Guyon's canal subtypes
  • Anatomy: C8-T1, lower trunk, medial cord; passes through the cubital tunnel (elbow) and Guyon's canal (wrist).
  • Motor NCS: record from ADM (G1 over the muscle belly, G2 3-4cm distal over the MCP joint) and/or FDIH, which may be more sensitive than ADM.
  • Four stimulation sites: wrist (adjacent to the FCU tendon), below elbow (3-4cm distal to the medial epicondyle), above elbow (10-12cm proximal to BE), and axilla.
  • Elbow position: use a flexed elbow (70-90 degrees) — more sensitive than extended for detecting ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
  • Measure across the elbow following the nerve's curved path — imprecise measurement here is a leading cause of technical error.
  • Abnormal: CV slowing >10 m/s across the elbow segment, or an absolute CV <50 m/s across the elbow.
  • Inching technique: 1-2cm segments across the below-elbow to above-elbow segment localize focal demyelination.
  • Guyon's canal types 1-5: Type 1 = combined motor+sensory; Type 2 = pure sensory; Type 3 = deep palmar + hypothenar motor; Type 4 = deep palmar motor only (hypothenar spared); Type 5 = distal deep palmar motor only (adductor pollicis, FDI).
  • The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist and is spared in Guyon's canal lesions.
Pearl: FDIH (first dorsal interosseous-hypothenar) may be more sensitive than ADM for detecting ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
17

Radial Nerve NCS

PIN, spiral groove, and axilla localization
  • Anatomy: C5-T1, all three trunks → posterior cord; exits the lateral wall of the axilla and wraps around the humerus in the spiral groove.
  • Three sensory nerves: posterior cutaneous (arm), lower lateral cutaneous (arm), posterior cutaneous (forearm).
  • Motor branches to triceps arise before the spiral groove, then to anconeus, brachioradialis, and ECRL.
  • PIN passes under the Arcade of Frohse, supplying ECR brevis, EDC, ECU, APL, EPL, EPB, and EIP.
  • Superficial radial sensory nerve travels subcutaneously next to the radius — susceptible to tight bands, watches, and handcuffs.
  • Motor NCS: record from EIP (G1 over the belly, G2 over the ulnar styloid); stimulate at the forearm, elbow, spiral groove, and above the spiral groove (near the axilla).
  • Sensory NCS: G1 over the anatomic snuffbox, G2 3-4cm distally on the thumb; stimulate 10cm proximal on the dorsal radius.
  • Spiral groove ("Saturday Night Palsy"): the most common site — wrist drop + finger drop, spared triceps, decreased dorsolateral hand sensation.
  • PIN neuropathy: wrist drop with radial deviation (ECRL spared), no sensory loss; entrapment at the Arcade of Frohse.
  • Axilla lesion (crutch palsy): same as spiral groove plus triceps weakness and posterior arm sensory loss.
Pearl: Wrist drop WITH radial deviation = PIN lesion (ECRL spared); wrist drop WITHOUT radial deviation = spiral groove or higher.
18

Tibial Nerve NCS

Abductor hallucis technique and the sural nerve gold standard
  • Sciatic nerve (L4-S2) splits into two nerves: common peroneal (posterior division, lateral) and tibial (anterior division, medial).
  • Tibial nerve: L5, S1, S2 roots; innervates the plantar flexors and inverters of the ankle.
  • Key muscles: medial gastrocnemius (S1-S2), lateral gastrocnemius (L5-S1-S2), soleus (S1-S2), tibialis posterior (L5-S1), FHL (L5-S1-S2), FDL (L5-S1-S2).
  • Motor NCS: record from abductor hallucis (belly-tendon method, two finger-widths distal to the navicular bone on the medial foot); stimulate at the ankle (posterior to the medial malleolus) and popliteal fossa.
  • Lateral plantar nerve: record from abductor digiti minimi on the lateral foot.
  • A CMAP ≥50% of the distal amplitude is acceptable with popliteal fossa stimulation.
  • Sural nerve is the gold standard lower-extremity sensory study; primarily tibial with some deep peroneal contribution; G1 posterior to the lateral malleolus, G2 3-4cm distal; stimulate midcalf at 14cm.
  • Medial/lateral plantar responses use an orthodromic method (G1 at the ankle, stimulate the plantar surface) with side-to-side comparison.
  • Tarsal tunnel syndrome: tibial nerve at the ankle, resembling carpal tunnel syndrome in presentation.
Pearl: The sural nerve is the gold standard for lower extremity sensory NCS.
19

Common Peroneal Nerve NCS

Deep vs superficial branches and the fibular head localization
  • L4, L5, S1 roots; bifurcates below the knee into deep and superficial peroneal nerves.
  • Deep peroneal: tibialis anterior, EHL, peroneus tertius, EDB, FDI of the foot; ankle dorsiflexion.
  • Superficial peroneal: peroneus longus/brevis, ankle eversion, sensation to the dorsum of the foot and lateral lower leg.
  • Motor NCS: record from EDB (belly-tendon); stimulate at the ankle, below the fibular head, and above the fibular head; CV ideally measured across that ~10cm segment.
  • Accessory deep peroneal nerve is present in up to 28%; a branch posterior to the lateral malleolus innervates the lateral EDB, producing a higher amplitude with proximal vs distal stimulation.
  • Sensory NCS: antidromic, G1 on the dorsum of the foot slightly lateral to midline, stimulating in the groove posterior to the peroneus longus insertion at 12-14cm.
  • Normal superficial peroneal sensory response + flaccid foot = demyelinating conduction block at the fibular head (axons intact).
  • Short head of biceps femoris is the only muscle above the knee innervated by the peroneal nerve — crucial for localizing peroneal vs sciatic lesions.
  • Normal short head biceps femoris EMG localizes the lesion to at or below the fibular head.
Pearl: Short head of biceps femoris is the KEY localizing muscle — abnormal means sciatic or higher; normal means peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head.
20

Median Nerve — Detailed NCS Protocol

CTS diagnosis, entrapment sites, and comparison techniques
  • Anatomy: C6-T1, lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.
  • Innervates pronator teres, forearm flexors (FCR, PL, FDS), the AIN branch (pure motor: FPL, FDP to digits 2-3, PQ), then through the carpal tunnel to APB and the thenar eminence.
  • Sensory: palm, thumb, index, middle, and lateral ring finger; thumb sensory maps to C6-C7, upper/middle trunk, lateral cord.
  • Motor NCS: record from APB (G1 one-third of the way from the metacarpal-carpal crease to the MCP joint, G2 4-5cm distal on the MCP joint), ground on the back of the hand; stimulate at the wrist (6.5-8cm proximal, between FCR and palmaris longus) and elbow.
  • Sensory techniques: orthodromic from the index finger, antidromic, palmar (8-10cm), and thumb orthodromic (C6-C7 assessment).
  • CTS diagnosis: sensory latency >4.0ms (digital), motor distal latency >4.4ms.
  • Comparison techniques: ring finger (median vs ulnar) and 2nd lumbrical vs 1st interosseous — both abnormal if the difference is >0.5ms.
  • Entrapment sites: Ligament of Struthers (rare), pronator syndrome (CV slowed across the proximal forearm, pronator teres itself normal), AIN syndrome (pure motor, can't make an "OK" sign), and CTS (most common EDX diagnosis).
  • CTS severity: Mild (symptoms only, borderline NCS); Moderate (atrophy, denervation, absent sensories); Severe (absent motor responses — needle EMG crucial).
Pearl: CTS is the most common diagnosis in the EDX lab. Sensory studies are the first to become abnormal and the most sensitive.
21

Facial Nerve and Blink Reflex

CN VII motor study, R1/R2 latencies, and clinical applications
  • Facial nerve (CN VII): motor to facial expression muscles; sensory carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
  • Course: brainstem → cerebellopontine angle → internal auditory meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → through the parotid → five branches.
  • Five branches: temporal (frontalis), zygomatic (orbicularis oculi), buccal (nasalis, orbicularis oris), marginal mandibular (mentalis), cervical (platysma).
  • Motor NCS: record from orbicularis oculi (or nasalis), reference on the opposite side, ground on the chin, stimulate at the stylomastoid foramen.
  • Normal: distal latency 3-4ms, amplitude 1-4 mV; side-to-side comparison is key — >50% amplitude drop or 20-30% latency prolongation is abnormal.
  • Bell's palsy: cranial mononeuropathy of CN VII affecting the entire side of the face; causes include GBS, ear trauma/infection, diabetes, CPA tumors, viral infection.
  • Blink reflex: polysynaptic; afferent = trigeminal (CN V, supraorbital branch), efferent = facial (CN VII).
  • R1 = 8-13ms, ipsilateral only (disynaptic); R2 = 28-42ms ipsilateral (polysynaptic); R2c = 29-44ms contralateral.
  • Applications: Bell's palsy evaluation (more sensitive than the facial motor study alone), early GBS detection, acoustic neuroma/CPA tumor diagnosis, MS diagnosis.
Pearl: R1 is ipsilateral only and the more reliable timing component. Blink reflex abnormalities may be the earliest detectable finding in GBS.
22

NCS Principles and Axonal vs Demyelinating Patterns

CMAP/SNAP fundamentals, conduction block, and the sural sparing pattern
  • CMAP: biphasic with an initial negative deflection; amplitude reflects the number of functioning motor axons plus muscle fiber integrity.
  • SNAP: represents large myelinated fiber function only — small fiber neuropathies can have entirely normal NCS.
  • CV calculation: distance between two stimulation points ÷ latency difference; e.g., 250mm ÷ 4.5ms = 55.6 m/s.
  • Axonal pattern: decreased CMAP/SNAP amplitudes, relatively preserved CV and distal latency (until severe), fibrillations/PSWs on needle EMG.
  • Demyelinating pattern: prolonged distal latencies, slowed CV, conduction block, temporal dispersion, absent/prolonged F-waves.
  • Conduction block: ≥50% drop in CMAP area or amplitude between distal and proximal stimulation; does NOT occur with pure axonal loss.
  • Late responses: F-waves = supramaximal, variable, backfiring of 1-5% of motor neurons; H-reflexes = submaximal, stable, true monosynaptic reflex.
  • CIDP shows a sural sparing pattern — sural SNAP preserved while median/ulnar SNAPs are abnormal — an important diagnostic clue.
Pearl: Conduction block (≥50% amplitude/area drop proximal vs distal) is the hallmark of acquired demyelination and does NOT occur with pure axonal loss.

HANDS-ON CLINICAL GUIDES

Step-by-step procedure workflows, troubleshooting, and practical tips for your first days in the lab

27. Step-by-Step: Setting Up & Performing a Motor NCS PRACTICAL GUIDE

StepActionDetails & Tips
1Check Skin TemperatureUse infrared thermometer. Hand ≥32°C, leg ≥30°C. If cold: warm with heating pad, warm towels, or warm-water soak for 5–10 min. Re-check BEFORE starting. Document the temperature.
2Prep the SkinLightly abrade with NuPrep or alcohol pad to reduce impedance below 5 kΩ. Excessive hair: shave a small patch. Clean off any lotion/oil. Dry skin is better than wet for electrode adhesion.
3Measure & Mark the DistanceUse tape measure. Mark 8 cm from E1 to distal stimulation site for ALL motor studies. Measure along the nerve course, not in a straight line. Mark with a skin marker.
4Apply Recording ElectrodesE1 (active) over the motor point (belly) of the target muscle. E2 (reference) on a nearby tendon or bony prominence. Apply conductive gel/paste. Secure with tape if using disc electrodes.
5Place Ground ElectrodeBetween stimulator and recording electrodes. Secure firmly. Good ground contact reduces stimulus artifact. Use strap or adhesive ground.
6Verify Machine SettingsMotor NCS defaults: Filters 2 Hz – 10 kHz, Sweep 2–5 ms/div, Sensitivity 2–5 mV/div. Adjust as needed during study.
7Start with LOW StimulusBegin at low intensity and gradually increase. Watch for a clear CMAP. Once you see a response, increase by 20–25% above the level that gives maximal amplitude = supramaximal stimulation.
8Check the WaveformMust have clean initial NEGATIVE (upward) deflection. If you see an initial POSITIVE (downward) deflection → E1 is off the motor point → STOP and reposition before collecting data.
9Record Distal ResponseCapture 3–5 consistent supramaximal responses. The machine will average or let you pick the best. Mark onset latency, baseline-to-peak amplitude, and negative-peak duration.
10Move to Proximal Stim SitesStimulate at each proximal site (elbow, axilla, Erb’s point, below/above fibular head, popliteal fossa). Use supramaximal stimulation at each site. Compare amplitudes for conduction block.
11Calculate CVCV = distance between two stim sites (mm) ÷ latency difference (ms). Use the ONSET latencies. Measure distance along the nerve path, not a straight line.
12Compare to Normal ValuesUse your lab’s normative data (age- and gender-adjusted if available). Flag: prolonged DL, low amplitude, slow CV, amplitude drop >50%, temporal dispersion.
Clinical tip: Your very first studies will be slower — that’s normal. Focus on getting clean waveforms with proper electrode placement before worrying about speed. Always look at the waveform morphology, not just the numbers. A beautiful waveform with a clean takeoff tells you your technique is good.

28. Step-by-Step: Performing a Sensory NCS (Antidromic) PRACTICAL GUIDE

StepActionDetails & Tips
1Verify TemperatureSame thresholds: hand ≥32°C, leg ≥30°C. Cold extremities are the #1 cause of absent or small SNAPs.
2Measure 14 cm DistanceALL sensory studies use 14 cm. Measure from E1 (recording electrode on the digit) to stimulation site. Mark clearly.
3Apply Ring ElectrodesE1 (active) = proximal ring on the recording digit. E2 (reference) = distal ring on same digit, 3–4 cm apart. Ensure snug fit with conductive gel. Too tight = patient discomfort; too loose = artifact.
4Adjust Machine SettingsSensory defaults: Filters 20 Hz – 2 kHz, Sweep 1–2 ms/div, Sensitivity 10–20 µV/div. SNAPs are MUCH smaller than CMAPs — increase sensitivity.
5Average Multiple ResponsesSNAPs are small (microvolts, not millivolts). Average 10–20 responses to improve signal-to-noise. More averaging = cleaner waveform. Some machines do this automatically.
6Measure Onset & Peak LatenciesOnset latency = where SNAP first leaves baseline (used for CV calculation). Peak latency = negative peak (used for comparison studies like CTS). Report BOTH.
7Measure AmplitudeBaseline-to-peak (most common) or peak-to-peak. Know your lab’s convention. Amplitude is the most variable sensory parameter — side-to-side comparison (>50% reduction = abnormal) is more useful than absolute values.
8Troubleshoot Absent SNAPsBefore calling it absent: (1) Re-warm the limb, (2) Reduce stimulus artifact (reposition ground), (3) Increase averaging (20–50 sweeps), (4) Check electrode contact, (5) Try shorter distance (10–12 cm). Age >70 = absent sural may be normal.
Antidromic vs orthodromic: Antidromic (stimulate proximally, record distally) gives LARGER SNAPs because the recording electrodes are right on the digit nerve. Orthodromic (stimulate digit, record at wrist) gives smaller SNAPs but less stimulus artifact. Most labs use antidromic for upper extremity and antidromic for sural. Your lab protocol determines which.

29. Troubleshooting Common Problems TROUBLESHOOTING

ProblemLikely CauseFix
Initial positive deflection on motor CMAPE1 is not over the motor point (belly of muscle)Move E1 toward the motor point. The CMAP should begin with a crisp upward (negative) deflection. This is the single most common beginner mistake.
Large stimulus artifact obscuring responsePoor ground contact; ground in wrong position; excessive stimulus currentReposition ground between stim and recording. Ensure good skin prep under ground. Reduce stimulus duration (0.1 ms). Rotate stimulator anode-cathode orientation. Clean/dry skin between electrodes.
No response / very small responseSubmaximal stimulation; cold limb; wrong nerve location; electrode not on muscle/nerveIncrease stimulus intensity. Check temperature and warm if needed. Verify electrode placement with anatomic landmarks. Try slight repositioning of stimulator (fan out/walk along nerve).
Waveform is “noisy” with wandering baseline60 Hz electrical interference; patient not relaxed; poor electrode contactEnsure patient is relaxed and muscles are not contracting. Check all electrode connections. Move or unplug nearby electrical devices. Use a 60 Hz notch filter if needed (last resort).
Unexpectedly slow CV or prolonged DLCold limb; incorrect distance measurement; wrong nerve stimulatedFIRST: check temperature! Cold = slow. Re-measure distances carefully. Verify you’re stimulating the correct nerve by confirming the expected muscle contracts.
CMAP larger at proximal than distal stim siteMartin-Gruber anastomosis (median motor) or accessory peroneal nerve (peroneal motor)This is an anatomic variant, NOT pathology. For Martin-Gruber: stimulate ulnar nerve to confirm crossover. For accessory peroneal: stimulate behind lateral malleolus to find the accessory component.
Patient reports excessive pain with stimulationStimulus intensity too high; dry electrodes; stimulating over scar tissue or bony prominenceStart at LOW intensity and increase gradually. Use adequate conductive gel on stimulator. Adjust stimulator position slightly. Reassure the patient — brief discomfort is normal.
Inconsistent/variable responsesSubmaximal stimulation; patient moving; electrode slippingEnsure you’re truly supramaximal (increase 20–25% above max). Ask patient to remain still. Re-tape any loose electrodes. Consistent hand pressure on stimulator.
Golden rule for your first week: If something looks wrong, it’s almost always a technical issue, not pathology. Check temperature, electrode placement, and stimulus intensity before interpreting findings as abnormal. When in doubt, repeat the study with fresh electrode placement.

30. Pre-Study Setup Checklist DAILY WORKFLOW

✓ItemDetails
□Review the clinical questionRead the ordering physician’s referral. What are they asking? CTS? Radiculopathy? Polyneuropathy? This determines which nerves and muscles to test.
□Brief clinical history & examAsk about symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness, pain). Duration? Distribution? Examine: strength, sensation, reflexes. This guides your study plan.
□Plan your study protocolDecide which NCS and EMG muscles you need BEFORE starting. For CTS: median motor + sensory, ulnar for comparison. For polyneuropathy: bilateral peroneal, tibial, sural + one upper extremity.
□Warm the room and patientRoom temperature 72–78°F (22–25°C). Have warming devices ready. Offer patient a blanket while waiting.
□Set up equipmentPower on EMG machine. Check electrode supplies (discs, rings, needles). Verify calibration. Have conductive gel, skin prep, tape, measuring tape, and skin marker ready.
□Position the patientSupine or seated comfortably. Arm/leg relaxed and supported. Remove watches, jewelry, bracelets from the tested limb.
□Explain the procedureBrief explanation: “small electrical impulses” and “a thin needle like an acupuncture needle.” Set expectations for mild discomfort. Answer questions.
□Check skin temperatureMeasure with infrared thermometer BEFORE starting. Warm if below threshold. Document temperature in your report.
Efficiency tip: Do all NCS first, then all EMG (needle exam). NCS with surface electrodes is less uncomfortable, so doing it first builds rapport before the needle portion. Start with the less-affected side if comparing bilaterally.

groups.title: Forearm & Wrist Landmarks — NCS Electrode Placement Reference

figures.alt: Forearm Flexor Muscles — Superficial, Intermediate & Deep Layers
figures.title: Forearm Flexor Muscles — Superficial, Intermediate & Deep Layers
figures.caption: Superficial layer: Pronator teres, FCR, Palmaris longus, FCU. Intermediate: FDS. Deep: FPL, FDP, Pronator quadratus. Clinical relevance: FCR and Palmaris longus tendons are landmarks for median nerve stimulation at the wrist (stimulate between them). FCU is the only ulnar-innervated superficial flexor.

figures.alt: Wrist Tendons — FCR, Palmaris Longus (PL) & FCU
figures.title: Wrist Tendons — FCR, Palmaris Longus (PL) & FCU
figures.caption: Radial to ulnar order at the wrist: FCR → PL → FCU. Critical NCS landmark: For median motor NCS, stimulate between FCR and PL tendons at the proximal wrist crease, 8 cm from E1 on APB. PL is absent in ~15% of people — if absent, stimulate just ulnar to FCR.

figures.alt: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) — Origin, Insertion & Innervation
figures.title: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris (FCU) — Origin, Insertion & Innervation
figures.caption: Origin: medial epicondyle. Insertion: pisiform, hook of hamate, 5th metacarpal. Action: wrist flexion + ulnar deviation. Innervation: Ulnar nerve (C7, C8). FCU is the ONLY ulnar-innervated superficial flexor — first muscle tested on EMG for cubital tunnel syndrome.

figures.alt: Medial & Lateral Epicondyles of the Humerus
figures.title: Medial & Lateral Epicondyles of the Humerus
figures.caption: Medial epicondyle: Key landmark for ulnar nerve stimulation at the elbow (below-elbow stim site). The ulnar nerve runs in the ulnar groove posterior to the medial epicondyle — palpate it with elbow flexed 70–90°. Lateral epicondyle: Origin of wrist/finger extensors (radial nerve territory).

figures.alt: Upper Limb Muscles — Anterior View, Superficial Layer
figures.title: Upper Limb Muscles — Anterior View, Superficial Layer
figures.caption: Proximal to distal: Coracobrachialis, biceps (short & long head), triceps (long head), brachialis, brachioradialis, pronator teres. Distal NCS landmarks: FCR, PL, FCU tendons at wrist. Flexor retinaculum = carpal tunnel roof. Know these layers for needle EMG insertion depth.

figures.alt: Median & Ulnar Nerve Courses in the Upper Limb
figures.title: Median & Ulnar Nerve Courses in the Upper Limb
figures.caption: Median nerve: From lateral + medial cords → runs with brachial artery down medial arm → antecubital fossa → between FDS heads → carpal tunnel → hand. Ulnar nerve: From medial cord → posterior to medial epicondyle (ulnar groove) → Guyon canal at wrist. These are the two nerves you stimulate for upper extremity motor and sensory NCS.

figures.alt: Brachial Plexus — Complete Diagram (Roots to Terminal Branches)
figures.title: Brachial Plexus — Complete Diagram (Roots to Terminal Branches)
figures.caption: Roots (C5-T1) → Trunks (Upper/Middle/Lower) → Divisions (Ant/Post) → Cords (Lateral/Posterior/Medial) → Branches. Mnemonic: Robert Taylor Drinks Cold Beer. Terminal branches: Musculocutaneous (lateral), Axillary + Radial (posterior), Median (lateral + medial), Ulnar (medial). Erb point (upper trunk) stimulation site for NCS.

groups.title: Radial Nerve — Course, Innervation & Injury Patterns

figures.alt: Radial Nerve Innervation — BEST Mnemonic
figures.title: Radial Nerve Innervation — BEST Mnemonic
figures.caption: BEST: Brachioradialis, Extensors of wrist/fingers, Supinators, Triceps. The radial nerve (C5-T1, posterior cord) is the nerve of extension. Injury = wrist drop + inability to extend fingers. Key EMG muscles: brachioradialis, ECR, EDC, triceps.

figures.alt: Radial Nerve — Sensory Distribution & Injury Patterns
figures.title: Radial Nerve — Sensory Distribution & Injury Patterns
figures.caption: Sensory: Posterior arm/forearm, dorsal hand (radial 3½ digits, proximal phalanges only). Common injuries: Humeral shaft fracture, Saturday Night Palsy (compression in radial groove), crutch palsy. Result: Wrist drop — a common EMG referral presentation.

figures.alt: The Radial Nerve — Complete Course, Muscles & Sensory Branches
figures.title: The Radial Nerve — Complete Course, Muscles & Sensory Branches
figures.caption: Full course: posterior cord → radial groove → splits at elbow into deep branch (PIN = motor: all finger/thumb extensors, supinator) and superficial branch (purely sensory to dorsal hand). PIN lesion: Finger drop WITHOUT wrist drop (ECRL and brachioradialis spared — they branch off above the split). This distinction matters for EMG localization.

groups.title: NCS Fundamentals — Motor vs Sensory Setup & Waveform Measurements

figures.alt: NCV Fundamentals - Motor vs Sensory NCS Setup
figures.title: NCV Fundamentals — Motor & Sensory Setup
figures.caption: Left (Motor): Stimulator at S1 (distal) & S2 (proximal), recording electrode (R) on muscle belly. Measures distal latency, proximal latency, amplitude (= axons), duration. CV = Distance / (Prox. lat. − Dist. lat.). Right (Sensory): Ring electrodes on digit, stimulator at wrist. Shows onset latency, peak latency, baseline-to-peak & peak-to-peak amplitude. Note the much smaller sensory amplitudes (µV vs mV).

figures.alt: Motor NCS - M Wave, CV Formula
figures.title: Motor NCS — M Wave & Conduction Velocity
figures.caption: M wave (CMAP): Waveform A shows proximal stimulation (longer latency 8.5 ms, amplitude 7 mV), waveform B shows distal stimulation (shorter latency 3.5 ms, amplitude 6.5 mV). CV = distance (270 mm) / latency difference (8.5 − 3.5 = 5 ms) = 54 m/s. Normal ranges: upper limb 45–70 m/s, lower limb 40–60 m/s. Slight amplitude drop from distal to proximal is normal (phase cancellation).

groups.title: Peroneal Motor NCS — Anatomy, Electrode Placement & Stimulation Sites

figures.alt: Lower Limb - Peroneal Nerve Branches and EDB
figures.title: Peroneal Nerve Anatomy — Branches & EDB
figures.caption: Common peroneal nerve at fibular head splits into deep peroneal (motor to EDB, tibialis anterior) and superficial peroneal (sensory). Note the accessory peroneal nerve coursing behind lateral malleolus — present in ~28% of patients. A (anode) and C (cathode) positions shown at stimulation sites. EDB (extensor digitorum brevis) is the recording muscle for peroneal motor NCS.

figures.alt: Peroneal Motor NCS - Measurement Diagram
figures.title: Peroneal Motor NCS — Measurement Setup
figures.caption: E1 on EDB belly, E2 distal on 5th MTP. Ground (Grd) between stimulator and recording electrodes. Distal stim site: ankle, 8 cm proximal to E1. Proximal stim at fibular head: anode (A) 4 cm proximal to cathode (C), positioned 2 cm distal to fibular head. These exact distances are critical for accurate CV calculation.

figures.alt: Peroneal Motor NCS - Clinical Setup with Stimulator
figures.title: Peroneal Motor NCS — Clinical Setup
figures.caption: Real clinical setup showing distal ankle stimulation. Stimulating electrodes (handheld stimulator) at ankle with cathode distal. Surface recording electrodes over EDB. Ground electrode on dorsum of foot between stimulator and recording site. Inset shows resulting CMAP amplitude waveform (5 mV scale). Note clean initial negative deflection confirming correct E1 placement over motor point.

figures.alt: Peroneal Motor NCS - Three Stimulation Sites
figures.title: Peroneal Motor — 3 Required Stimulation Sites
figures.caption: (A) Ankle stimulation: Cathode 8 cm proximal to G1 (E1 on EDB), G2 (E2) distal, ground between stim and recording. (B) Below fibular head (BFH): Cathode just distal to fibular head — often requires higher current (nerve is deep here). (C) Above fibular head / popliteal fossa: Cathode above fibular head, 10–12 cm proximal to BFH site. All 3 sites needed to assess for fibular head compression (most common peroneal neuropathy site). Compare CV across fibular head segment to distal segment.

figures.alt: Sural Sensory NCS - Electrode Placement
figures.title: Sural Sensory NCS — Antidromic Setup
figures.caption: G1 (E1) posterior to lateral malleolus. G2 (E2) 3–4 cm distal. Cathode on posterolateral calf, 14 cm proximal to G1. Ground between cathode and G1. Patient prone or lateral decubitus. Key clinical pearl: sural SNAP is normal in radiculopathy (pre-ganglionic lesion preserves peripheral axon) but abnormal in plexopathy (post-ganglionic). Normal: peak latency ≤4.5 ms, amplitude ≥4 µV.

groups.title: Median Nerve — Wrist Anatomy & Motor NCS Setup

figures.alt: Median Nerve Anatomy at Wrist - FCR PL APB Branches
figures.title: Median Nerve Anatomy at Wrist
figures.caption: Critical landmarks for NCS: median nerve passes between FCR (flexor carpi radialis) and PL (palmaris longus) tendons at the distal wrist crease — this is your wrist stimulation site. The nerve enters the hand through the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel) and gives off: (1) recurrent motor branch to APB (your E1 recording target), (2) digital sensory branches, (3) motor branches to lumbricals 1–2. PL is absent in ~14% of patients — use FCR as the primary landmark.

figures.alt: Median Motor NCS - APB Electrode Placement with Distances
figures.title: Median Motor NCS — APB Recording Setup
figures.caption: E1 on thenar eminence over APB motor point (midway between wrist crease and 1st MCP). E2 on proximal phalanx of thumb. Ground on palm. Wrist stimulation (A=anode, C=cathode) between FCR and PL, 7 cm from E1 (some labs use 8 cm). The recurrent branch of median N. is shown — E1 must be directly over where this branch enters APB for a clean initial negative deflection. An initial positive = E1 too lateral or distal.

figures.alt: Median Motor NCS - All Stimulation Sites Along Arm
figures.title: Median Motor — All Stimulation Sites
figures.caption: Complete median motor NCS setup showing E1 on APB, E2 on thumb, and 4 stimulation sites along the median nerve: (1) wrist — between FCR and PL; (2) antecubital fossa — medial to biceps tendon and brachial artery; (3) upper arm; (4) Erb point / axilla. Routine studies use wrist + elbow; axilla and Erb point added when proximal pathology suspected (brachial plexopathy, thoracic outlet). Ground placed mid-forearm between stim and recording.

groups.title: Ulnar Motor NCS — ADM Recording & Both Motor Sites on One Hand

figures.alt: Ulnar Motor NCS - ADM Electrode Placement
figures.title: Ulnar Motor NCS — ADM Recording Setup
figures.caption: E1 on hypothenar eminence over ADM (abductor digiti minimi) belly. E2 on 5th MCP joint. Ground on palm. Wrist stimulation: cathode (C) 8 cm proximal to E1, lateral to FCU tendon on medial wrist. Note TWO stimulation levels at wrist shown — the more proximal pair is for comparison studies. For the standard study: wrist (8 cm), below elbow (3–4 cm distal to medial epicondyle), above elbow (10 cm proximal to BE site, elbow flexed 70–90°).

figures.alt: Both APB and ADM Recording Sites on One Hand
figures.title: Quick Reference — Both Motor Recording Sites
figures.caption: Single-image reference showing both motor recording setups on one hand. Upper pair: Median motor — E1 on thenar eminence (APB), E2 on thumb base. Lower pair: Ulnar motor — E1 on hypothenar eminence (ADM), E2 on 5th MCP. Note the positions relative to each other — thenar is radial side, hypothenar is ulnar side. In practice, you’ll place one set, run that nerve, then move electrodes for the next nerve. Ground stays on the dorsum or palm.

groups.title: Sensory NCS — Median & Ulnar Antidromic to Digit 4 (CTS Comparison)

figures.alt: Median and Ulnar Sensory NCS to Digit 4 - Ring Electrodes
figures.title: Median & Ulnar Sensory — Antidromic to Digit 4
figures.caption: Key CTS comparison technique. Ring electrodes E1 (active) and E2 (reference) on digit 4. Ground on palm. Both median N. and ulnar N. stimulated at wrist, 14 cm proximal to E1. Since digit 4 receives dual innervation (median radial side, ulnar ulnar side), comparing the two latencies eliminates interpatient variability. A median–ulnar latency difference ≥0.5 ms = abnormal (suggests CTS). Standard antidromic sensory to digit 2 (median) or digit 5 (ulnar) uses the same ring electrode setup and 14 cm distance.

figures.alt: Martin-Gruber Anastomosis - Median to Ulnar Crossover Anatomy
figures.title: Martin-Gruber Anastomosis — Crossover Anatomy
figures.caption: Present in 15–20% of patients. Median nerve fibers cross over to the ulnar nerve in the forearm, then innervate ulnar-supplied hand muscles (usually FDI, sometimes ADM). E1 on FDI (1st dorsal interosseous), E2 on thumb. When present: median CMAP at elbow may be LARGER than at wrist (crossover fibers travel via ulnar nerve distally); ulnar CMAP at above-elbow may be larger than below-elbow. Can mimic conduction block — always consider M-G before diagnosing block!

figures.alt: Martin-Gruber Anastomosis Waveforms - Normal and with CTS
figures.title: Martin-Gruber Waveforms — Recognition Patterns
figures.caption: Top: M-G with normal median nerve — wrist stim gives a normal CMAP, but elbow stim shows an initial positive deflection (crossover fibers arrive at FDI via the ulnar nerve, approaching E1 from a different direction). Bottom: M-G with CTS — wrist stim shows delayed/dispersed CMAP (slowed through carpal tunnel), while elbow stim CMAP appears larger and sharper (crossover fibers bypass the tunnel via the ulnar nerve). This pattern can be misread as proximal conduction block if M-G is not recognized.

groups.title: Median Motor NCS — Clinical Stimulation Technique

figures.alt: Median Motor NCS - 3 Stimulation Sites Clinical Photos
figures.title: Median Motor — 3 Stimulation Sites
figures.caption: (a) Wrist stimulation: Stimulator held with cathode distal, pressed firmly between FCR and PL tendons. Recording electrodes (red/black leads) visible on thenar eminence. Ground pad on palm. (b) Elbow (antecubital fossa): Stimulator placed medial to biceps tendon over the median nerve. (c) Above elbow / upper arm: Stimulator on medial arm. Note the stimulator hand grip and angle — cathode always points TOWARD the recording electrodes (distal).

figures.alt: Median Motor NCS - Close-up of Recording Electrodes on Thenar Eminence
figures.title: Recording Electrodes — Thenar Close-up
figures.caption: Close-up of the actual recording electrode pads placed on the hand for median motor NCS. Active electrode (E1) on the thenar eminence over APB belly. Reference electrode (E2) more distal on the thumb/1st metacarpal area. Note the small round adhesive disc electrodes connected via snap leads — this is how it looks in practice. The electrodes should be positioned to give a clean initial negative (upward) deflection. If you see an initial positive, move E1 slightly toward the muscle belly.

groups.title: Peroneal & Tibial Motor NCS — Clinical Stimulation Technique

figures.alt: Peroneal Motor NCS - 3 Stimulation Sites Clinical Photos
figures.title: Peroneal Motor — 3 Stimulation Sites
figures.caption: (a) Ankle: Stimulator on dorsal ankle, 8 cm proximal to E1 on EDB. Recording electrodes visible on foot (E1 on EDB, E2 on 5th MTP). (b) Below fibular head (BFH): Stimulator pressed against lateral leg just distal to fibular head — higher current often needed here as the nerve is deeper. (c) Above fibular head / popliteal: Stimulator on posterolateral knee area. Be careful not to co-stimulate the tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa — if AH twitches, reposition more laterally.

figures.alt: Tibial Motor NCS - Ankle and Popliteal Stimulation Clinical Photos
figures.title: Tibial Motor — 2 Stimulation Sites
figures.caption: (a) Ankle (posterior to medial malleolus): Stimulator placed behind the medial malleolus over the tibial nerve, 8 cm from E1 on AH. Recording electrodes on medial foot (E1 on AH — 1 cm proximal and inferior to navicular). (b) Popliteal fossa: Stimulator pressed into the mid-popliteal fossa over the popliteal pulse. REMEMBER: a 21–50% amplitude drop between ankle and popliteal is NORMAL for tibial motor — do NOT call this conduction block. It’s expected phase cancellation over the long nerve segment.
